title: Rent Payment
bodyText: Tenant shall pay Landlord monthly rent of {{monthly_rent}} (Monthly Rent) in advance on the due date specified in this Lease, without demand, deduction, or setoff, except as permitted by applicable law. If the due date falls on a weekend or legal holiday, rent is due on the next business day.

title: Late Fee
bodyText: If Tenant fails to pay Monthly Rent in full within {{late_fee_grace_days}} days after it is due, a late fee of {{late_fee_amount}} will be assessed. Acceptance of a late payment does not waive Landlord's right to require full payment of Rent on the date it is due or to pursue any other remedy available under this Lease.

title: Returned Checks / Dishonored Payments
bodyText: If any payment of Rent is returned for insufficient funds or otherwise fails, Landlord may require that the payment be replaced by a cashier's check, certified check, or money order, and may charge Tenant a fee associated with the failed payment, not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law. If more than two of Tenant's payments during the Term are returned for insufficient funds, Landlord may require all future payments of Rent be made by cashier's check, certified check, or money order.

No conflict with this clause's generic mechanics; the actual NSF cap lives in Title 6 general banking law (§6-08-16), not landlord-tenant law, and isn't restated here. | KS CHECKED 2026-08-30 (v59 canvass): K.S.A. 60-2610(g) caps the service charge on a dishonored check at $30. This clause's unqualified 'any fee associated with the failed payment' was flagged as a possible conflict, since unlike landlords-access and holdover it carries NO self-limiting 'to the extent permitted by applicable law' language. TAYLOR'S DECISION: leave as is, no KS override. Reasoning: 60-2610(g) caps the charge the drawee/vendor imposes, and under this clause the landlord recovers that charge as a pass-through loss rather than setting its own fee, so the effective ceiling is $30 either way. See edu-nsf-fee-cap-ks. | Also confirmed for KS: no payment-method fee ban (no analog to N.D.C.C. 47-16-20.1); Kansas does not restrict charging for particular payment methods. | MN re-audit 2026-09-03: MN's returned-check fee cap identified (Minn. Stat. §604.113, $30 service charge) — see edu-returned-check-fee-cap-mn. NO CLAUSE EDIT MADE and no MN override created: this clause does not hardcode a dollar figure, so it does not conflict with the cap, matching the disposition WY reached for the same situation. §5a.1 JUDGMENT: the finding is STATE-DRIVEN (each state's bad-check statute differs — WY $30, MN $30, KS/NE/ND/SD各 their own), but requires no shared-clause change because the clause is figure-agnostic. Flagged instead: the clause's phrase 'may charge Tenant any fee associated with the failed payment' is unbounded on its face and could read as authorizing more than the statutory cap in every tagged state. NOT edited here — it is tagged CO;WY;KS;NE;MN;ND and a rewording triggers §5a.1 across six states. Recommend a scoped shared-clause pass. | SHARED-CLAUSE PASS 2026-09-03 (§5a.1). TRIGGER: every one of the six tagged states has a cap and a row recording it (CO nsf-fee-limit-co; WY edu-returned-check-fee-cap-wy; KS edu-nsf-fee-cap-ks; NE edu-bad-check-restitution-vs-nsf-fee-ne; ND edu-returned-check-fee-cap-nd; MN edu-returned-check-fee-cap-mn, $30 under §604.113). The unbounded word 'any' was therefore wrong in all six simultaneously — a clause that promised landlords something no tagged state allows. | SD ADDED 2026-09-07 (SD re-audit, Tier A of the L.2 exhaustive generic-clause audit). State-driven, not uniform. Self-limiting - 'not to exceed the maximum amount permitted by applicable law' - so it survived the 57A-3-421 amendment from $40 to $60 without carrying a hardcoded figure. The clause that deferred held; the education row that hardcoded broke. | OH: no statutory cap. §1319.16's $30-or-10% ceiling binds a COLLECTION AGENCY (§1319.12(A)(2) excludes a landlord collecting its own account) and does not apply. 'Maximum permitted by applicable law' therefore resolves to no cap — state an actual amount. §5321.14 unconscionability is the only ceiling.

bodyText: All payments received shall be applied first to outstanding fees, charges, costs, utilities, or other amounts due under this Lease, and then to base rent, unless otherwise required by applicable law. Nothing in this provision limits any statutory right Tenant may have to cure nonpayment of base rent.

A fees-first allocation that left the rent itself unpaid would collide with that; the row's own sentence preserving the tenant's statutory right to cure nonpayment of rent is what keeps it lawful in NV - do not remove it.

title: Late Fee Limit
bodyText: Any late fee assessed under this Lease will not exceed the greater of $50.00 or 5% of the amount of Rent past due, and no late fee will be assessed until at least 7 days after Rent is due, as required by Colorado law. Landlord will provide Tenant written notice of any late fee within 180 days after the date the related Rent payment was due.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-105(1)(a) [7-day floor], (1)(b) [$50/5% cap], (1)(c) [must be disclosed in the rental agreement], (1)(j) [180-day written notice requirement], (7) [late fee distinct from rent, cross-refs § 13-40-104(1)(d)]. RESOLVED 2026-09-13. $50/5%/7-day figures CONFIRMED CURRENT and always have been in this section - § 38-12-105 was created whole by SB 21-173 (ch. 349, L. 2021, eff. 2021-10-01); no subsequent raise. (Correcting the prior round's note: the $25/5% figure traced to a committee amendment on the unrelated 2020 bill HB20-1141, not this section's own history - that was a false lead.) Real content gap found and fixed: the clause omitted (1)(j)'s requirement that written notice of the late fee be given within 180 days after the due date - added to bodyText as the landlord's own commitment. (1)(c)'s in-agreement-disclosure requirement is why this clause needs to exist at all (already satisfied by its existence, no further action). (7)'s late-fee-distinct-from-rent rule is already independently reflected in default-by-tenant's carve-out. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: NSF Fee Limit
bodyText: If any payment under this Lease is dishonored or returned unpaid, Tenant will be responsible for a reasonable returned-payment charge, consistent with Colorado's dishonored-instrument statute (C.R.S. 13-21-109), plus any actual bank charges Landlord incurs. This charge is not Rent, is not subject to any late fee applicable to Rent, and will not be characterized as Rent for purposes of any remedy available for nonpayment of Rent.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 13-21-109. Corrected 2026-08-27 re-audit from a wrong citation (13-40-107(4), the notice-to-quit statute) and a fabricated $20 flat cap; reframed as a reasonable, non-Rent charge under the dishonored-instrument statute. Re-confirmed 2026-09-13 (Claude Browser follow-up): still no statutory $20 CO landlord NSF cap found anywhere; the conservative self-limiting rewrite remains the defensible position. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

Under s1671(d) a liquidated-damages provision is VOID, except that the parties may agree on an amount presumed to be the damage 'when, from the nature of the case, it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage.' Two consequences the old text got backwards: (1) the default is voidness, not validity; (2) the burden flips - under (b) the party attacking the clause must prove it unreasonable, while under (d) the landlord must bring the clause within the exception. The new body text is drafted to track (d)'s exception language rather than the (b) standard. s1671(a) yields to any other statute expressly prescribing a liquidated-damages rule for the contract - none found for residential late fees in the sections read, but note s1950.5 expressly governs security, so deposit-forfeiture provisions route there and not through s1671. NOT CONFIRMED: the old row's assertion that 'California does not set a statutory cap on late fees' is consistent with everything read this pass but is NOT a full-chapter proof-of-absence - no dedicated late-fee cap search was run. Do not upgrade that limb to CITED without one. Also unread: Orozco v. Casimiro and Del Monte Properties v. Dolan are the cases usually cited for applying s1671(d) to residential late fees; both are pointers only, neither has been read. EXTEND SCREEN 2026-09-19: now supersedes the base row `late-fee`, which is blocked for CA. s1951.5 RESOLVED 2026-09-19 (primary text supplied): it reads in its entirety 'Section 1671, relating to liquidated damages, applies to a lease of real property.' CONFIRMATORY, NOT CORRECTIVE, as predicted - s1671(c)(2) already reached a lease of real property for use as a dwelling on its own terms, and s1951.5 removes any argument that s1671 is confined to contracts for goods and services. No change to this row's analysis; the earlier flag is cleared. MILITARY TENANTS, added 2026-09-19: Mil. & Vet. Code s403(b) - no fine or penalty accrues during a court stay of an action to enforce the lease, and a court may relieve a service member from a late fee incurred while in service if military service materially impaired their ability to pay. title: NSF Fee Limit
bodyText: If Tenant pays rent or any other amount due under this Lease by check, draft or order for payment and it is not honored for lack of funds, because Tenant has no account with the drawee, or because Tenant stops payment, Tenant shall be liable to Landlord for the amount of the payment and a service charge of {{nsf_fee}}, not to exceed $25 for the first such instrument and $35 for each subsequent one. No service charge is owed if Tenant stopped payment to resolve a good faith dispute with Landlord, if Tenant provides written confirmation from Tenant's financial institution that the instrument was returned due to an error by that institution, or if Tenant provides written confirmation that the account had insufficient funds because of a delay in a regularly scheduled direct deposit of a social security or government benefit assistance payment.
notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 against Civ. Code s1719(a) (primary text supplied by Taylor). Figures CONFIRMED - $25 first, $35 each subsequent 'to that payee' - but the prior dormant row carried three defects. (1) FRAMING: it said the cap applies 'as required by California law'. s1719(a)(1) is a statutory ENTITLEMENT capped at those amounts, not a requirement to charge. Third CA row found reciting a landlord option as a legal mandate, after month-to-month-notice-ca and the CO entry-notice precedent. (2) INSTRUMENT SCOPE - the substantive defect. The old row capped the fee for any 'dishonored or returned payment'. s1719(a)(6) defines the trigger as making, uttering, drawing or delivering a CHECK, DRAFT OR ORDER for the payment of money upon a bank or depository that refuses to honor it. A returned ACH debit or a declined card is not obviously an instrument drawn by the tenant, so s1719 may not reach electronic payment methods at all. That cuts both ways: the old row asserted a statutory safe harbour over payment types the statute may not cover, and for those types a returned-payment fee in a residential lease is an ordinary liquidated-damages provision governed by s1671(d) - VOID unless actual damages were impracticable or extremely difficult to fix. See late-fee-safe-harbor-ca; the two rows are now linked by that analysis. Clause scoped to checks, drafts and orders accordingly. (3) OMITTED EXCEPTIONS: s1719(a)(3) good-faith-dispute stop payment, where the payee recovers only on CLEAR AND CONVINCING evidence that no good faith dispute existed; (a)(4) written confirmation of financial institution error; (a)(5) written confirmation that the shortfall came from a delayed direct deposit of SOCIAL SECURITY OR GOVERNMENT BENEFIT ASSISTANCE. A flat fee clause misstates the law against benefit recipients in particular. All three now in body text. Note s1719(a)(6)(C): a STOP PAYMENT counts as passing a check on insufficient funds, subject to the good-faith-dispute carve-out. CROSS-CHAPTER: s1719 sits in Part 3, Obligations Imposed by Law - outside the landlord-tenant title. Instruction 7 pattern, fourth confirmation in CA. EXTEND SCREEN 2026-09-19: now supersedes the base row `returned-payments`, which is blocked for CA. s1719 NOW READ IN FULL 2026-09-19 - three additions. (1) TREBLE DAMAGES, s1719(a)(2): after a written demand by CERTIFIED MAIL stating the section's provisions, the check amount and the service charge, the drawer has 30 DAYS to pay; failing that, liability becomes the unpaid check amount PLUS TREBLE that amount, not less than $100 nor more than $1,500, in place of the service charge. (2) EXCEPTIONS to the service charge: a STOP PAYMENT in a good-faith dispute (payee must prove no good-faith dispute by clear and convincing evidence, s1719(a)(3), (b)); written confirmation of BANK ERROR (a)(4); and a delayed SOCIAL SECURITY or government benefit deposit (a)(5). For a stop payment, the demand must be in the prescribed s1719(c) form, sent certified with a receipt in evidence (d), and the payee must show a reasonable effort to reconcile before suing (e). s1719(j)(2): liability arises only ONCE per check. (3) NO POSTDATED-CHECK EXCLUSION anywhere in s1719 - candidate 427.4's North Dakota trap does not exist here. The ACH/card scope caveat stands: every limb is framed around a 'check, draft, or order'.

title: Services & Utilities Provided by Landlord
bodyText: Landlord will provide only the services and utilities expressly specified in this Lease, and as otherwise required by applicable law. Landlord is not liable for any interruption or insufficiency of a service or utility resulting from causes beyond Landlord's reasonable control.
notes: CO added - verified this session (statute walk + full-library audit; content itself unchanged WY added 2026-08-21 (full-library cross-check pass): generic mechanics, no CO-specific statutory language or number, confirmed no conflict with WY findings from this project. | KS note: 'Tenant waives all liability of Landlord' language is exculpation-flavored, same category of soft spot as tenants-property-insurance. Extended to KS applying the same risk-tolerance precedent Taylor set for that clause (K.S.A. 58-2547(b): unenforceable-only unless knowing use of a known-prohibited term is shown) — not re-flagged as a fresh open item, but documented here in case Taylor wants to revisit the whole category at once. | NE extended (session 2, whole-library generic-clause audit): generic mechanics, no NE-specific statutory language or number, confirmed no conflict with NE findings from this project. | States KS removed (session 5, full liability-audit fix): superseded by state-specific override(s) addressing K.S.A. 58-2547(a)(4)/(a)(1) and/or Neb. Rev. Stat. §76-1415(1)(d) exposure found in this session's full-library liability audit. | MN extended (Minnesota session, whole-library audit): generic mechanics compatible; note MN's habitability covenant (§ 504B.161, subd. 1(5)) requires heat at a minimum of 68°F Oct 1–Apr 30, which this clause's 'as otherwise required by applicable law' language already covers. | CORRECTION (Minnesota session, whole-library audit): MN tag added earlier this session was premature and has been REMOVED. This clause contains an exculpatory liability-waiver sentence ('Tenant waives all liability of Landlord for any interruption...') matching the pattern KS and NE found PROHIBITED under their general prohibited-lease-provisions statutes (§ 58-2547, § 76-1415), and which WY only confirmed safe after directly reading all 11 sections of its own Article 12. Minnesota's statute walk this session did NOT find a single consolidated 'prohibited lease provisions' statute like CO/KS/NE — instead MN has scattered per-section non-waiver rules — but that is not the same as a confirmed absence of a general exculpatory-clause prohibition, which may exist elsewhere in MN law (consumer protection statutes, case law) outside Chapter 504B. Leaving MN untagged until checked directly, consistent with WY's methodology rather than assuming safety from silence. | NE RE-AUDIT 2026-08-31 — REWORDED, and the diagnosis differs from the one flagged going in. §76-1415(1)(d) read from primary source (nebraskalegislature.gov): it bars exculpation or limitation of landlord liability 'arising due to ACTIVE AND ACTIONABLE NEGLIGENCE of the landlord.' This clause is already self-limited to 'causes beyond Landlord's reasonable control,' and a cause beyond the landlord's reasonable control is by definition not the landlord's active and actionable negligence — so the ORIGINAL NE SESSION'S REASONING ON (d) WAS CORRECT and no gross-negligence carve-out is needed here. That is why this clause differs from tenants-property-insurance-ne, parking-ne, and storage-space-ne: those three carried BLANKET disclaimers with no limiting qualifier, so they genuinely needed the carve-out. The apparent 'fixed four of five' asymmetry is not an oversight; the fifth clause needed a different and smaller fix. THE REAL EXPOSURE IS §76-1415(1)(a), NOT (d): the phrase 'TENANT WAIVES all liability of Landlord' is a tenant-side waiver, and (a) bars a rental agreement providing that the tenant 'agrees to waive or to forego rights or remedies under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act.' Even where the practical scope is narrow, waiver-framed language invites the (a) argument for free. Recast as an allocation ('Landlord is not liable') rather than a tenant waiver. Substance unchanged; exposure removed. §5a.1 PROPAGATION JUDGMENT — UNIFORM, not state-driven. Applied to all three tagged states (CO;WY;NE). CO: §38-12-801(3) voids waivers of quiet enjoyment and of good faith and fair dealing, so waiver-framed phrasing is mildly worse there too — the reword is beneficial. title: Default by Tenant
bodyText: Tenant will be in default under this Lease if Tenant fails to pay Rent when due and does not cure the failure within the time period specified by applicable law after receiving written notice from Landlord. Tenant will also be in default if Tenant fails to comply with any other obligation under this Lease and does not cure the failure after receiving written notice. Except as required by applicable law, Tenant's failure to pay an assessed late fee, apart from the underlying Rent itself, will not by itself entitle Landlord to terminate this Lease or pursue eviction. If Tenant is in default, Landlord may exercise all rights and remedies available under applicable law, including terminating this Lease, regaining possession of the property, and recovering unpaid Rent, late fees, and reasonable costs and expenses, less amounts obtained from the Security Deposit. Landlord will use reasonable efforts to mitigate damages resulting from Tenant's default to the extent required by applicable law. To the extent permitted under applicable law, the prevailing party may recover from the other party court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees and expenses incurred in connection with any legal proceedings related to this Lease.
notes: CO added - verified this session (statute walk + full-library audit; content itself EDITED this session | CORRECTED 2026-08-20 (caught by Claude CLI review): added explicit carve-out that an unpaid late fee alone cannot trigger termination/eviction, consistent with CO law that a late fee is distinct from rent and cannot be grounds for eviction on its own. WY added 2026-08-21 (full-library cross-check pass): generic mechanics, no CO-specific statutory language or number, confirmed no conflict with WY findings from this project. | MN extended (Minnesota session, CO;WY-scoping resolution): cure-period language defers to 'applicable law' rather than hardcoding a number, so it doesn't shorten any MN statutory cure right (MN has no general statutory cure period for lease violations, confirmed absent this session). Fee-shifting sentence is already mutual ('prevailing party') — compatible with MN's automatic-mutuality rule (§504B.172), no conflict. | Cross-state plain-language cleanup (Minnesota session, follow-up to MN's plain-language audit): long compound sentence split into shorter ones, no substantive change. Not a legal requirement for this clause's other tagged states (only MN's Plain Language Contract Act, Minn. Stat. §325G.31, was confirmed to apply this project) — done as a general readability improvement since the pattern was found library-wide, not MN-specific. | ND extended (North Dakota session 1, CO;WY-maintenance-scoping review resolved by reading the full CO and MN decision logs directly): defers to 'applicable law' for cure timing, no ND-specific conflict. Fee-shifting language ('prevailing party') matches N.D.C.C. § 47-16-13.6 exactly, which awards attorney's fees 'to the prevailing party' -- mutual, not one-way. This resolves ND's piece of the standing fee-shifting-mutuality question (though the broader cross-state consolidation across CO/WY/KS/NE/MN remains a separate open item). | 5a.1 RETROACTIVE CLASSIFICATION 2026-08-28: the prevailing-party attorney-fee rewrite here was STATE-DRIVEN (forced by C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a)(II)), not uniform, and was inherited by WY/MN/ND/SD without classification - the exact failure mode 5a.1 exists to prevent. Checked for WY 2026-08-28: WY has NO reciprocity statute (see edu-no-fee-reciprocity-wy), so a landlord-only clause would be enforceable there and the mutual language is a voluntary giveaway. Taylor's decision 2026-08-28: KEEP mutual language for WY. MN, ND, and SD remain unclassified for this edit. | CROSS-STATE FEE-SHIFTING CONSOLIDATION COMPLETED 2026-09-06 (ND re-audit). The standing open item -- 'is this clause's fee language genuinely mutual, and does it work in every tagged state?' -- is resolved. Operative sentence: 'To the extent permitted under applicable law, the prevailing party may recover from the other party court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees and expenses incurred in connection with any legal proceedings related to this Lease.' FIVE DISTINCT STATE ARCHITECTURES, not one question: (1) CO -- a landlord-only fee clause is VOID and the lease must be drafted mutual; 'prevailing party' SATISFIES this. (2) MN -- fee clauses are made mutual BY OPERATION OF LAW regardless of lease text; consistent, no conflict. (3) KS (K.S.A. 58-2547) and NE (§ 76-1415(1)(c)) -- attorney-fee clauses are BANNED OUTRIGHT in either direction; this clause is correctly NOT tagged to either, and a library-wide check confirmed ZERO LEASE_CLAUSE rows tagged KS or NE contain attorney-fee language. (4) ND -- § 47-16-13.6 awards fees to 'the prevailing party' by statute; clause language matches exactly. (5) WY -- American Rule, no reciprocity statute, contract governs. OPEN FLAG FOR WYOMING, surfaced not resolved: per edu-no-fee-reciprocity-wy the Wyoming Supreme Court requires a contract to 'unequivocally provide' for fee recovery before fees may be awarded. This clause hedges twice -- 'TO THE EXTENT PERMITTED UNDER APPLICABLE LAW' makes the entitlement conditional on an external referent, and 'MAY recover' is permissive rather than mandatory. Under a strict unequivocal-provision standard that phrasing may not suffice, which would leave a WY landlord with NO fee recovery in a state whose default is that each side bears its own. No Wyoming case applying the standard to comparable hedged language was located, and no edit is made on that basis -- flagged for Taylor. Note the hedge exists for a reason: it is what makes the clause safe to share with CO and MN. Any WY fix should be a WY-specific override, NOT an edit to the shared text. | WYOMING FLAG RETRACTED 2026-09-06 after reading the actual case law rather than this library's characterisation of it. NO WY-SPECIFIC OVERRIDE IS NEEDED. The Wyoming standard is EXPRESS CONTRACTUAL AUTHORISATION, not a heightened magic-words test: Cowardin v. Finnerty (Wyo. 1999) -- 'absent statutory or contract language expressly authorizing recovery of attorney fees, parties are responsible for payment of their own attorney fees'; Emken, 2006 WY 112, ¶ 8 -- 'a prevailing party may be reimbursed for its attorney fees when express statutory or contractual authorization exists'; Thorkildsen v. Belden, 2012 WY 8; Circle Resources v. Hassler, 2023 WY 22, ¶ 8 -- 'A prevailing party may, however, be reimbursed for attorneys' fees when provided for by contract or statute.' The Wyoming failure cases are ones where the contract said NOTHING about fees. Cowardin is explicit: 'Given the absence of any reference to attorney fees in the purchase agreement, Sellers were not entitled to recover attorney fees.' THIS CLAUSE EXPRESSLY REFERS TO ATTORNEY FEES, NAMES THE PREVAILING PARTY, AND USES THE COURT'S OWN FORMULATION. The supposed defect -- 'may recover' being permissive -- is the verb the Wyoming Supreme Court itself uses in stating the rule. 'To the extent permitted under applicable law' is a savings clause; no Wyoming authority was located suggesting a savings clause defeats otherwise-express authorisation, and the circularity concern raised earlier in this session was speculative. PROCESS NOTE: the flag originated from this library's own edu-no-fee-reciprocity-wy row, which characterises the standard as requiring a contract to 'unequivocally provide' for fees. The cases say 'expressly authorizing' / 'express... authorization'. Raising a structural change to a four-state shared clause on a secondary characterisation, without reading the cases, was the Addendum L.5 failure committed in the same session that wrote L.5. No CA conflict found. | NV: Read in full 2026-09-24 against NRS 118A (revisor text Rev. 4/15/2026, 2025 session incorporated). Applies as written: promises a cure opportunity for every non-rent breach, more generous than 118A.430 (5 days for remediable breach; none for a breach that cannot be remedied) - lawful. Prevailing-party fee sentence is the form 118A.220(1)(c) permits. PROVISIONAL pending NRS Ch. 40 read. | NV (text batch 2, 2026-09-24): PROVISIONAL CLEARED. NRS 40.2516: 5-day perform-or-quit, lease saved by performing within 5 days, no notice if the breach cannot be cured; NRS 40.2514: 3-day notice to surrender with NO cure for unauthorized assignment/sublet, waste, unlawful business, nuisance, or controlled-substance violations (other than simple possession). The clause promises a cure for every non-rent breach - more than NV requires for 40.2514 grounds; lawful, but a product choice worth knowing. NRS 40.252: a landlord may not shorten statutory notice periods by contract - the clause defers to law, so no conflict.

title: Early Termination
bodyText: Tenant may terminate this Lease before the end of the Term by providing Landlord at least 30 days' written notice. Tenant will pay an early termination fee equal to one month's Rent ({{monthly_rent}}) or 30% of the remaining Rent due under the Term, whichever is greater, and remains responsible for Rent and other obligations up to the termination date. Landlord may terminate this Lease early by providing Tenant at least 30 days' written notice if Tenant breaches a material term of this Lease and fails to cure the breach within 10 days of receiving written notice, or if Tenant vacates or abandons the property without notifying Landlord. Nothing in this Section limits any right either party has under applicable law. This includes a Tenant's right to terminate without penalty due to active military service under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, due to the property becoming uninhabitable through no fault of Tenant, or — except as prohibited by law in the case of a Tenant's death — any other termination right or limitation provided by applicable law.

title: Holdover Tenancy
bodyText: If Tenant does not vacate the property by the end of the Term, Landlord may pursue any remedy allowed by applicable law to recover possession. Landlord will also be entitled to recover from Tenant holdover damages in the maximum amount permitted by applicable law for each day Tenant remains in possession after the end of the Term. Alternatively, Landlord may accept Tenant's continued payment of Rent, in which case this Lease will be deemed to continue on a month-to-month basis on the same terms and conditions, terminable by either party upon written notice as required by applicable law.

Rev. Stat. §76-1437(3) allows up to 3x periodic rent or 3x actual damages for willful bad-faith holdover — higher than this clause's double-rent figure, so the clause still holds up in NE without an override (per Taylor's read, Flag 6). See edu-holdover-ne for the full NE figure and a note to revisit the double-rent baseline once more states are surveyed. | MN extended (Minnesota session, whole-library audit): generic mechanics, already vetted against KS/NE's prohibited-lease-provisions statutes (the strictest bar found in this project to date) since this clause was already tagged KS;NE; no MN-specific statutory language or number identified in this session's statute walk that conflicts. No exculpatory/liability-waiver language present. | Cross-state plain-language cleanup (Minnesota session, follow-up to MN's plain-language audit): long compound sentence split into shorter ones, no substantive change. Not a legal requirement for this clause's other tagged states (only MN's Plain Language Contract Act, Minn. Stat. §325G.31, was confirmed to apply this project) — done as a general readability improvement since the pattern was found library-wide, not MN-specific. | SHARED-CLAUSE PASS 2026-09-03 (§5a.1). EDIT: removed the hardcoded 'double the Monthly Rent ... or the maximum amount allowed under applicable law, if less' and replaced it with a pure deferral to the statutory maximum. §5a.1 JUDGMENT: **STATE-DRIVEN** — the holdover figure genuinely differs per state — but the EDIT itself is uniform-safe and no per-state override is required, because each state's figure is already carried by its own education row. WHY THE OLD TEXT WAS WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, which is why leaving it was not an option: (1) OVER-PROMISED in MN — Minnesota has NO holdover multiplier at all (§504B.141 and the eviction chapter, confirmed at MN re-audit), so 'double the Monthly Rent' described a remedy that does not exist; the self-limiting tail made it lawful but misleading. (2) UNDER-CLAIMED in NE — Nebraska allows three months' periodic rent or threefold actual damages, whichever is greater, PLUS statutory attorney fees (§76-1437(3)), all of which EXCEED double monthly rent. The old 'or the maximum allowed ... if less' language could only ever cap DOWNWARD, so a Nebraska landlord relying on the clause would recover materially less than the statute allows. A ceiling-only formulation silently forfeits recovery in any state whose statutory figure is higher than the hardcoded one. KS is unaffected either way (1.5x cap under K.S.A. 58-2570(c), already below double, per edu-holdover-ks). GAP SURFACED, NOT CLOSED: CO and WY have NO holdover-damages education row and their statutory figures have never been verified in this project. The 'double' figure appears to have originated as Colorado's, but that has not been confirmed against C.R.S. Recommend verifying CO and WY holdover figures and adding edu-holdover-co / edu-holdover-wy, matching KS/NE/MN. | FOLLOW-UP 2026-09-03: the gap flagged in the shared-clause pass is now closed, and the answer is worse than expected. THE 'DOUBLE THE MONTHLY RENT' FIGURE HAD NO STATUTORY BASIS IN ANY OF THE FIVE TAGGED STATES. CO: no multiplier, damages = reasonable rental value (§13-40-123, Behr v. Burge). WY: no multiplier, actual damages plus 10% interest (§1-21-1211(b), provisional). KS: 1.5x cap, BELOW double (K.S.A. 58-2570(c)). NE: three months' periodic rent or threefold actual plus attorney fees, ABOVE double (§76-1437(3)). MN: no multiplier at all. So the number was wrong in every direction simultaneously — too high in three states, too low in one, and baseless in the two where it was assumed to have originated. The shared-clause pass hypothesized it 'appears to have originated as Colorado's'; that hypothesis is now DISPROVED. It appears to be generic template boilerplate that entered the library before any state research and was never questioned, and it survived four state re-audits. Removing it was correct. Recording the provenance because it is the clearest example in the project of an unsourced number propagating through a shared clause: nothing in the library ever asserted where 'double' came from, and every state's own research quietly contradicted it.

title: Month-to-Month Termination Notice
bodyText: Either party may terminate a month-to-month tenancy by written notice served as provided in Code of Civil Procedure section 1162 or by certified or registered mail. Tenant must give notice at least as long as the period of the tenancy (30 days for a month-to-month tenancy), regardless of how long Tenant has resided at the property. Landlord must give at least 60 days' written notice, except that 30 days' notice is sufficient if Tenant has resided at the property for less than one year, or if the conditions in Civil Code section 1946.1(d) are met (unit separately alienable, sold to a natural-person bona fide purchaser in escrow, notice given within 120 days of escrow, no prior notice given, and purchaser intends to reside there at least one year). Landlord's notice must include the statutory abandoned-property statement required by Civil Code section 1946.1(h). Where this property is subject to Civil Code section 1946.2, notice alone is not sufficient: after the qualifying occupancy period Landlord must also state a just cause for termination.
notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 from primary text of Civ. Code s1946.1. The pre-existing dormant row was defective in four ways: (1) it applied the 30/60 split to BOTH parties - s1946.1(b) imposes 60 days on the OWNER only; a tenant's notice is one tenancy period regardless of occupancy length, so the old text bound a long-term tenant to a 60-day duty CA law does not impose, while reciting 'as required by California law'; (2) it omitted the s1946.1(d) bona-fide-purchaser 30-day path entirely; (3) it omitted the s1946.1(h) abandoned-property statement the owner's notice must contain; (4) it was silent on the s1946.2 just-cause overlay, so for a covered unit it told the tenant the tenancy could be ended on notice alone, which is false. Same error shape as the CO entry-notice 'as required by Colorado law' correction.

title: Lead-Based Paint Disclosure
bodyText: LEAD WARNING STATEMENT. Housing built before 1978 may contain lead-based paint. Lead from paint, paint chips, and dust can pose health hazards if not managed properly. Lead exposure is especially harmful to young children and pregnant women. Before renting pre-1978 housing, lessors must disclose the presence of known lead-based paint and/or lead-based paint hazards in the dwelling. Lessees must also receive a federally approved pamphlet on lead poisoning prevention. Landlord's disclosure: [state either that Landlord has no knowledge of lead-based paint or lead-based paint hazards in the dwelling, or describe all known lead-based paint and lead-based paint hazards]. Records and reports: [state either that Landlord has no reports or records pertaining to lead-based paint or lead-based paint hazards in the dwelling, or list all available records and reports and confirm they have been provided to Tenant]. Tenant acknowledges receipt of the information above and of the federally approved pamphlet Protect Your Family from Lead in Your Home. Landlord and Tenant each certify, to the best of their knowledge, that the information they have provided is true and accurate.

No exculpatory/liability-waiver language present. | PART 5 PRIMARY-TEXT READ 2026-08-27 (Taylor supplied full C.R.S. 38-12-503): MATERIAL CORRECTION (federal spot-check). 40 CFR 745.113(b)(1) requires the Lead Warning Statement to appear VERBATIM in the lease; the prior clause paraphrased it, which does not satisfy the regulation. Replaced with the exact regulatory text (federal regulatory text is a government edict, not copyrighted). Also added the other elements 745.113(b) requires: landlord's affirmative disclosure or statement of no knowledge (b)(2), the records/reports list or statement of none (b)(3), tenant's acknowledgment of receipt (b)(4), and the accuracy certification (b)(6). Exposure for noncompliance is meaningful: 42 U.S.C. 4852d(b)(5) statutory penalty inflation-adjusted to $22,263 per violation (24 CFR 30.65(b)), plus treble damages and fees. NOTE: the 10-day inspection opportunity is a SALE requirement and correctly absent here. title: Bed Bug Disclosure
bodyText: Information about Bed Bugs. Bed bug Appearance: Bed bugs have six legs. Adult bed bugs have flat bodies about 1/4 of an inch in length. Their color can vary from red and brown to copper colored. Young bed bugs are very small. Their bodies are about 1/16 of an inch in length. They have almost no color. When a bed bug feeds, its body swells, may lengthen, and becomes bright red, sometimes making it appear to be a different insect. Bed bugs do not fly. They can either crawl or be carried from place to place on objects, people, or animals. Bed bugs can be hard to find and identify because they are tiny and try to stay hidden. Life Cycle and Reproduction: An average bed bug lives for about 10 months. Female bed bugs lay one to five eggs per day. Bed bugs grow to full adulthood in about 21 days. Bed bugs can survive for months without feeding. Bed bug Bites: Because bed bugs usually feed at night, most people are bitten in their sleep and do not realize they were bitten. A person's reaction to insect bites is an immune response and so varies from person to person. Sometimes the red welts caused by the bites will not be noticed until many days after a person was bitten, if at all. Common signs and symptoms of a possible bed bug infestation: • Small red to reddish brown fecal spots on mattresses, box springs, bed frames, mattresses, linens, upholstery, or walls. • Molted bed bug skins, white, sticky eggs, or empty eggshells. • Very heavily infested areas may have a characteristically sweet odor. • Red, itchy bite marks, especially on the legs, arms, and other body parts exposed while sleeping. However, some people do not show bed bug lesions on their bodies even though bed bugs may have fed on them. For more information, see the Internet Web sites of the United States Environmental Protection Agency and the National Pest Management Association. Tenant shall report any suspected bed bug infestation to Landlord promptly and in writing, using the following procedure: {{bed_bug_reporting_procedure}}.
notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 against Civ. Code s1954.603 (primary text supplied by Taylor). Statute requires the information 'in substantially the following form' and in AT LEAST 10-POINT TYPE - shipped effectively verbatim because 'substantially' is not a licence to compress. THIRD type-size floor found in CA (8-point at s2079.10a, 10-point here, 12-point at s1946.2(f)(3)); the schema still cannot express any of them. The prior dormant row was a four-line paraphrase and had two substantive defects beyond omitting the entire prescribed block: (1) it promised 'Landlord's process for investigating a suspected infestation' - s1954.603(b) requires the opposite, the procedure for the TENANT TO REPORT to the landlord, which is why this row now carries a landlord-supplied {{bed_bug_reporting_procedure}} field; (2) it asserted the notice covers 'the danger of self-treating with pesticides' - NO SUCH ELEMENT EXISTS in s1954.603. That element appears in other states' bed-bug statutes, so this is the Instruction 18 error shape (another state's architecture imported as fact) sitting inside a shipped CA row. Timing: duty attaches on and after 2017-07-01 prior to creating a NEW tenancy. The separate one-time catch-up duty to notify all existing tenants by 2018-01-01 is spent and is deliberately not modelled. s1954.601 defines 'pest control operator' as a Branch 2 licensee of the Structural Pest Control Board. GAP: s1954.600 was not supplied and has not been read - likely legislative findings, but unconfirmed. No penalty or private remedy appears anywhere in ss1954.601-1954.605 as supplied; enforcement route unknown and NOT researched.

[If a local health officer has issued a remediation order affecting this property and no notice requiring no further action has since been received, state that fact here and attach a copy of the order to this Lease; otherwise state 'Landlord has received no remediation order affecting this property under Health and Safety Code section 25400.22 or 25400.25.'] Tenant acknowledges in writing receipt of this notice and of a copy of any pending order. notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 against H&S s25400.28 (primary text supplied by Taylor; Chapter 6.9.1, amended by Stats. 2019 ch. 691 (AB 1596), eff. 2020-01-01). The chapter is 6.9.1, not 6.9.2 as I guessed. Five defects in the prior dormant row. (1) TRIGGER WRONG: the row keyed off 'an order prohibiting occupancy due to methamphetamine contamination that has not been satisfied'. The statute keys off a REMEDIATION ORDER under ss25400.22/25400.25, and the duty runs until the owner receives a s25400.27 notice that the property requires NO FURTHER ACTION. An occupancy prohibition is not the trigger. (2) FENTANYL OMITTED: the chapter has covered methamphetamine OR FENTANYL since AB 1596 took effect 2020-01-01. The row was meth-only and is retitled - six years stale. (3) TIMING: s25400.28(b) attaches the duty to all prospective tenants WHO HAVE COMPLETED A RENTAL APPLICATION, earlier than lease signing. The row modelled it purely as a lease disclosure, so the duty could be missed entirely for an applicant who never reaches signature. (4) FREE TEXT IS NOT COMPLIANCE: the statute requires four mechanical things - written notice, A COPY OF THE ORDER provided, the tenant's WRITTEN ACKNOWLEDGMENT before signing, and the notice ATTACHED to the rental agreement. The old '[describe any known contamination order]' bracket satisfies none of them. This is document assembly, not clause text - same class of problem as the s1632 translation duty. (5) REMEDY OMITTED: if the owner does not comply with (b), THE PROSPECTIVE TENANT MAY VOID THE RENTAL AGREEMENT. Severe, and absent from the old row. OUT OF SCOPE, flagged not resolved: s25400.28(c) is a separate stricter regime for a mobilehome, manufactured home or recreational vehicle subject to an order - it may not be sold, rented OR OCCUPIED until notice of all meth or fentanyl laboratory activities and any remediation is given, with notice and order attached to the rental agreement, and (c)(4) gives the same void right. Consistent with the standing mobilehome-park deprioritization. Subdivision (a) is the sale-side duty and is not our concern.

title: Mold Disclosure
bodyText: If Landlord knows, or has reasonable cause to believe, that mold is present at the property in an amount that may exceed exposure limits recommended by a health authority, Landlord must disclose that condition to Tenant in writing, as required by California law. Landlord discloses: [describe any known mold condition, or state 'none known'].
notes: CA: STILL INACTIVE after reading H&S s26147 (primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19). The row asserts a live disclosure duty; the statute's own commencement clause may mean no such duty has ever taken effect. s26147(e): 'The requirements of this section shall not apply until the first January 1 or July 1 that occurs at least six months after the department adopts standards pursuant to Sections 26103 and 26105 AND develops guidelines pursuant to Section 26130.' The operative trigger in (a) is likewise defined by reference to the s26103 permissible exposure limits or the s26105 health-threat guidelines. VERIFIED FROM TEXT: the duty is contingent and self-suspending. NOT VERIFIED: whether the department ever adopted those standards and guidelines - that is a factual question outside the section text and is the single thing needed to close this row. It is widely reported that the PELs were never adopted, but this project has been burned by widely reported, so it stays open. This is a NEW ERROR SHAPE for the checklist, adjacent to the s2924.85 repeal: a statute that is on the books, correctly cited, and still not in force. Other limbs read and captured for whenever it does commence: (b) no duty to conduct air or surface testing; (c)(1) disclosure to prospective tenants before entering the agreement and (c)(2) to current tenants in affected units as soon as reasonably practical; (d) exemption where the mold was remediated per the s26130 guidelines. NOTE the (a) trigger reaches mold 'both visible and invisible or hidden'. SEPARATE AND UNREAD: Civ. Code s1941.1(a)(7) is reported to place visible mold in the habitability list, which would make mold actionable in CA regardless of s26147's status. Not read this pass - pull it before concluding CA has no mold obligation. CORRECTION 2026-09-19: my earlier pointer to Civ. Code s1941.1(a)(7) as the mold limb was WRONG - (a)(7) is garbage and rubbish receptacles. The real route is the OPENING WORDS of s1941.1(a), read section-open: a dwelling is untenantable if it substantially lacks the listed characteristics OR IS A RESIDENTIAL UNIT DESCRIBED IN H&S s17920.3 OR s17920.10. That incorporation is confirmed from the text. Whether s17920.3 actually lists visible mold growth as a substandard condition is NOT confirmed - s17920.3 has not been read. NEEDED: H&S s17920.3. The supplied s1941.1 text also stopped at (a)(7), so (a)(8) onward is unread. RESOLVED 2026-09-19 on the habitability limb: H&S s17920.3(a)(13) (read section-open; amended by Stats. 2024 ch. 487 (SB 1465), eff. 2025-01-01) DOES list 'Visible mold growth' as a substandard condition, and Civ. Code s1941.1(a) incorporates s17920.3 by reference. So California DOES have a live mold obligation - it is a HABITABILITY duty, not a disclosure duty. This row is a disclosure clause and stays INACTIVE: the s26147 disclosure duty remains contingent under s26147(e) and the only question left on it is factual, whether the department ever adopted the s26103/s26105 standards and s26130 guidelines. Two limits on the habitability route that matter and are easy to overstate: (1) visible mold growth must be 'as determined by a health officer or a code enforcement officer, as defined in Section 829.5 of the Penal Code' - it is NOT self-executing on a tenant's or landlord's own assessment; (2) it EXCLUDES mold that is minor and found on surfaces that can accumulate moisture as part of their properly functioning and intended use (shower surrounds and the like). The s17920.3 preamble adds a further threshold: the condition must exist to an extent that endangers life, limb, health, property, safety or welfare. s17920.10, the OTHER s1941.1(a) incorporation, READ 2026-09-19 - it governs lead hazards, not mold, so it does not affect this row. See edu-lead-hazards-ca. FACTUAL QUESTION RESOLVED 2026-09-19: the s26147(e) predicate standards were NEVER ADOPTED. Primary source: CDPH's own 2005 Report to the Legislature on implementing the Toxic Mold Protection Act concluded that science-based permissible exposure limits for indoor mold could not be established, and CDPH's 2017 Statement on Indoor Dampness and Mold confirms the scientific basis for that conclusion had not changed as of 2015 and that no federal or state policy sets safe exposure limits. The SB 655 (2015) Senate floor analysis quotes the same CDPH position. Consistent secondary sources through 2026 report no PELs adopted. So s26147 has NEVER COMMENCED and this row correctly stays INACTIVE - now VERIFIED as not in force, the same posture as foreclosure-disclosure-ca. WORTH NOTING: at least one 2026 secondary source describes s26147 as operative with a 'practical trigger' of visible mold - the exact misreading s26147(e) forecloses. Another secondary-source error of the kind this project was built to catch. Residual limit: CDPH's primary statements run to 2017; post-2017 status rests on consistent secondary reporting and the absence of any contrary source.

title: Flood Disclosure
bodyText: Flood Hazard Disclosure. [If Landlord has actual knowledge that the property is located in a special flood hazard area or an area of potential flooding, state that fact here; otherwise state 'Landlord has no actual knowledge that the property is located in a special flood hazard area or an area of potential flooding.'] Tenant may obtain information about hazards, including flood hazards, that may affect the property from the Internet Web site of the Office of Emergency Services, including the MyHazards tool at {{myhazards_url}}. Landlord's insurance does not cover the loss of Tenant's personal possessions, and it is recommended that Tenant consider purchasing renter's insurance and flood insurance to insure Tenant's possessions from loss due to fire, flood, or other risk of loss. Landlord is not required to provide additional information concerning the flood hazards to the property, and the information provided pursuant to Government Code section 8589.45 is deemed adequate to inform Tenant.
notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 against Gov. Code s8589.45 (primary text supplied by Taylor, current as of 2026-01-01). STRUCTURAL DEFECT CORRECTED - rule_type moved CONDITIONAL -> REQUIRED. The prior dormant row treated the WHOLE disclosure as conditional on the property being in a flood zone. It is not: s8589.45(a) requires the disclosure in EVERY residential lease entered into on or after 2018-07-01, and only element (a)(1) carries the 'if the owner has actual knowledge' qualifier. Elements (a)(2), (3) and (4) are unconditional. As previously modelled, a non-flood-zone CA property would have received NO disclosure at all. Four further defects in the old text: (1) it omitted element (a)(2) entirely, including the statutory requirement that the disclosure CONTAIN the MyHazards Internet Web site address; (2) it omitted element (a)(4), the landlord safe harbour; (3) it narrowed element (a)(3) to 'renter's insurance covering flood damage' - the statute requires stating that the owner's insurance does not cover the tenant's possessions AND recommending both renter's and flood insurance against fire, flood or other risk of loss; (4) it glossed the trigger as a 'special flood hazard area as designated by the Federal Emergency Management Agency' - the statute says 'special flood hazard area OR AN AREA OF POTENTIAL FLOODING' and never mentions FEMA, so the row imported a narrower federal definition the statute does not use. ACTUAL KNOWLEDGE is defined, not left at large - s8589.45(a)(1)(A)-(C): written notice from any public agency, the mortgage holder requiring flood insurance, or THE OWNER CURRENTLY CARRYING FLOOD INSURANCE. The third is the one landlords overlook: carrying the policy is itself actual knowledge. This belongs in the builder as a question, not as landlord free text. Prescribed floor: NO SMALLER THAN EIGHT-POINT TYPE. s8589.45(b) subjects the disclosure to Civ. Code s1632 - SECOND statute in CA carrying the translation duty after s1946.2(f)(3). OPEN: {{myhazards_url}} is an app-config value, not landlord input. The statute requires the address to appear; the current CalOES MyHazards address has NOT been verified from primary source this pass and must be confirmed and maintained at sync - a hardcoded URL is exactly the kind of value that rots silently.

NRS 118A.275 (Added 2009, 2791; no amendment in the source line). (1) duty runs to a PROSPECTIVE tenant - so disclosure must precede the lease; (2) a WILLFUL violation is a deceptive trade practice for purposes of NRS 598.0903-598.0999 - NOT itself a stated misdemeanor, confirming the old note that the penalty had been overstated. title: Sex Offender Registry Notice
bodyText: Notice: Pursuant to Section 290.46 of the Penal Code, information about specified registered sex offenders is made available to the public via an Internet Web site maintained by the Department of Justice at www.meganslaw.ca.gov. Depending on an offender's criminal history, this information will include either the address at which the offender resides or the community of residence and ZIP Code in which the offender resides.
notes: CA: VERBATIM STATUTORY TEXT - Civ. Code s2079.10a(a)(3), primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19 (Amended by Stats. 2018, ch. 907 (AB 1289), eff. 2019-01-01). Prescribed floor: NOT LESS THAN 8-POINT TYPE. Do not add a preamble, reword, or drop the URL. The prior dormant row was a PARAPHRASE and dropped four operative elements: the 'Notice:' opener, the Penal Code s290.46 citation, the www.meganslaw.ca.gov address (the only actionable content in the notice), and the precise 'address at which the offender resides' / 'community of residence and ZIP Code in which the offender resides' phrasing. It also prepended 'As required by California law, Landlord provides Tenant the following notice:' to prescribed text. Same failure shape as the federal Lead Warning Statement correction in the CO re-audit. SCOPE - rule_type set to CONDITIONAL, not REQUIRED, and this is a judgment call to overturn if you disagree: s2079.10a(a) reaches leases of SINGLE-FAMILY residential real property and leaseholds in multiunit property with MORE THAN FOUR dwelling units. A lease of a unit in a 2-4 unit building falls between the two limbs and is NOT covered. The old row was REQUIRED with no scope condition, so it rendered on duplex/triplex/fourplex leases as legally mandated when it is not. Shipping the bare statutory notice on an uncovered property is harmless surplusage; reciting that it is required is not. Paragraphs (a)(1) and (a)(2) are historical - the (a)(1) form governs contracts entered 1999-07-01 to 2005-08-31 and references the repealed Penal Code s290.4 database and a '900' line; (a)(2) is the transition window. Only (a)(3) applies to contracts entered on or after 2006-04-01. Do not ship (a)(1). LANDLORD SAFE HARBOUR, not yet its own row: s2079.10a(b) provides that delivery of the notice discharges any duty to supply further information about the proximity of registered offenders, and gives a registered offender no cause of action against the disclosing party; s2079.10a(c) preserves all other existing duties. CROSS-CHAPTER: this section sits in Title 6, ch. 3, art. 2 ('Duty to Prospective Purchaser of Real Property') - entirely outside the Civ. Code s1940 et seq. landlord-tenant provisions. Instruction 7 pattern confirmed for CA. SECOND type-size floor found in CA after s1946.2(f)(3)'s 12-point requirement. COUNTERPART, added 2026-09-19: Pen. Code s290.46(j) PROHIBITS using the website's information for housing decisions except to protect a person at risk - so the landlord must tell tenants about the site but must not use it to choose them. See edu-megans-law-housing-use-ca.

title: Termination Notice (Property Exempt from For-Cause Requirements)
bodyText: Either Landlord or Tenant may terminate a periodic tenancy under this Lease at the end of a tenancy period, or elect not to renew a fixed-term tenancy at the end of the term, by serving written notice that expires at the end of that period or term. The required notice depends on how long the tenancy has run: at least 91 days for a tenancy of one year or longer; at least 28 days for a tenancy of six months or longer but less than a year; at least 21 days for a tenancy of one month or longer but less than six months; at least 3 days for a tenancy of one week or longer but less than one month, or a tenancy at will; and at least 1 day for a tenancy of less than one week. The notice must describe the property and the particular date the tenancy will terminate, and must be signed by the party giving it or their agent or attorney. Because [describe the applicable exemption here - see C.R.S. section 38-12-1302(1)(a), (1)(b), (1)(d), (1)(e), or (1)(f)], this tenancy is not subject to Colorado's for-cause eviction requirements under C.R.S. section 38-12-1301 et seq.

notes: CO: GENERIC. Generic mechanics, not asserted as statute-derived. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Electric Vehicle Charging System - End of Tenancy
bodyText: A charging system installed at Tenant's expense remains Tenant's property. Upon termination of this Lease, if the charging system is removable, Tenant may remove it, or sell it to Landlord or another tenant at an agreed price - Landlord is under no obligation to purchase it. Tenant is responsible for any damage to the property or the charging system resulting from its removal, consistent with this Lease's Surrender at End of Term Section.
notes: CO: GENERIC. Generic mechanics, not asserted as statute-derived. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Late Fee - Tenant Receiving a Housing Subsidy
bodyText: If Tenant's Rent is paid in whole or in part by a housing subsidy program, Landlord will not impose a late fee against Tenant for the late payment or nonpayment of any portion of Rent that the subsidy provider, rather than Tenant, is responsible for paying, as required by Colorado law.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-105(1)(f). RESOLVED 2026-09-13: real rule is a total prohibition on charging a late fee on the subsidy-covered portion of rent, not a $20 cap. Verbatim: a landlord shall not 'Impose a late fee on a tenant... for the late payment or nonpayment of any portion of the rent that a rent subsidy provider... is responsible for paying.' The stray $20 likely traces to a $20 PENALTY figure in introduced SB 21-173 (now $50 under § 38-12-105(3)) - a penalty, not a fee cap, mistranscribed. bodyText rewritten to state the actual prohibition; verified against the shipped clauseTemplates.js. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Habitability Proration - Tenant Receiving a Housing Subsidy
bodyText: If Tenant's Rent is paid in whole or in part by a housing subsidy program and the property becomes partially uninhabitable, Rent will be proportionally reduced based on the portion of the property affected, calculated on the total Rent for the property including both the tenant-paid and subsidy-paid portions. If Rent has already been paid for the affected period, Tenant will receive a prorated refund, as required by Colorado law.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-507; amended by HB25-1240 (ch. 291, L. 2025). Confirmed (Claude Browser follow-up, 2026-09-13). Caveat: a Senate floor amendment attempted to exclude the subsidy-paid portion from proration; DRE's post-enactment summary says reimbursement applies regardless of who paid (implying the amendment did not carry), but this rests on the summary, not the enrolled text. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Radon Disclosure
bodyText: Residential real property may present exposure to dangerous levels of indoor radon gas, which may place occupants at risk of developing radon-induced lung cancer. The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment strongly recommends that all tenants have an indoor radon test performed before leasing residential real property, and recommends having radon levels mitigated if elevated concentrations are found. Elevated radon concentrations can be reduced by a radon mitigation professional. Landlord discloses the following regarding radon testing, concentrations, or mitigation systems at the property, if known: [describe any known radon testing results, concentrations, or mitigation systems, or state 'none known']. Tenant acknowledges receipt of this disclosure and the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment's radon brochure, attached to this Lease, as required by Colorado law.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-803. Confirmed (Claude Browser follow-up, 2026-09-13). The companion 180-day/one-year-lease remedy (edu-radon-lease-length-co) is at (3)(b) per an earlier pass, not independently re-confirmed this round. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Service and Assistance Animals
bodyText: A service animal or other assistance animal that Tenant or an Occupant needs as a reasonable accommodation for a disability is not considered a pet under this Lease, regardless of any pet policy, breed, weight, or size restriction stated elsewhere in this Lease. Landlord will not charge a pet deposit, pet rent, or other pet-related fee for an assistance animal. If the disability and the disability-related need for the animal are not readily apparent, Landlord may request reliable documentation confirming the need for the accommodation, to the extent permitted by applicable law; if the disability and need are readily apparent, Landlord will not require such documentation. Tenant remains responsible for any damage to the property caused by an assistance animal. Landlord may deny or withdraw this accommodation if the specific animal poses a direct threat to the health or safety of others, or would cause substantial physical damage to the property, that cannot be reduced or eliminated by another reasonable accommodation.

title: Service and Assistance Animals
bodyText: A service animal or other assistance animal that Tenant or an Occupant needs as a reasonable accommodation for a disability is not considered a pet under this Lease, regardless of any pet policy, breed, weight, or size restriction stated elsewhere in this Lease. Landlord will not charge a pet deposit, pet rent, or other pet-related fee for an assistance animal. If the disability and the disability-related need for the animal are not readily apparent, Landlord may request reliable documentation confirming the need for the accommodation, but will not require details about the nature or severity of Tenant's disability beyond what is necessary to verify the need for the accommodation, as required by Colorado law. If the disability and need are readily apparent, Landlord will not require such documentation. Tenant remains responsible for any damage to the property caused by an assistance animal. Landlord may deny or withdraw this accommodation if the specific animal poses a direct threat to the health or safety of others, or would cause substantial physical damage to the property, that cannot be reduced or eliminated by another reasonable accommodation. Tenant is hereby warned, as required for enforcement under Colorado law, that intentionally misrepresenting an animal as a service animal or assistance animal to obtain a right or privilege under this Section is unlawful under C.R.S. sections 18-13-107.3 and 18-13-107.7, punishable by escalating fines.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 24-34-502 (CADA); § 18-13-107.3; § 18-13-107.7; HB 16-1426 (eff. 2017-01-01); HB 21-1271. CADA (not HUD/FHA) is CO's independent basis, unaffected by HUD's 2025-09-17 ESA guidance withdrawal or its 2026-05-22 enforcement narrowing. Corrected 2026-08-28: misrepresentation mischaracterized as always criminal - 18-13-107.3 (housing) is a civil infraction; only 18-13-107.7 (public accommodations) remains a petty offense. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Notice of Habitability Rights
bodyText: Every tenant is entitled to safe and habitable housing under Colorado's warranty of habitability, as described in this Lease's Maintenance & Repairs Section. Colorado law prohibits Landlord from retaliating against Tenant in any manner for reporting an unsafe or uninhabitable condition, exercising any right under this Lease, or participating in a tenant organization. To report a condition that may affect the habitability of the property, Tenant should provide written notice to Landlord at: [insert landlord's designated WRITTEN habitability-notice address, e.g. email address or mailing address - do not designate a phone number or any verbal method].
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-503(3)(f)(II), (3)(e); Anderson v. Shorter Arms Investors, LLC, 2023 COA 71, 537 P.3d 831. Corrected 2026-08-27: a bracket prompt suggesting a phone number as the notice channel would have waived the landlord's own right to written notice under (3)(f)(II); rewritten written-only with a warning. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Utility Allowance with Tenant-Paid Overage
bodyText: Landlord's obligation to pay for [specify utility, e.g. water and sewer] under this Lease's Utilities Paid by Landlord Section is limited to [insert monthly utility allowance amount] per month. If the actual utility cost for a given month exceeds this amount, Tenant will reimburse Landlord for the excess within [insert number of days, e.g. 15] days of receiving a copy of the utility provider's bill showing the actual charges for that month. This reimbursement is a separate obligation from Rent: it is not subject to any late fee applicable to Rent under this Lease, will not be characterized as Rent for purposes of any remedy available for nonpayment of Rent, and Landlord's remedies for Tenant's failure to pay it are limited to those otherwise available under this Lease for breach of an obligation other than Rent.
notes: CO: NOT_STATUTE. Explicitly NOT statute-derived - 'sourced from Taylor's own observation, not the statute walk.' No citation applies. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Security Deposit Paid in Installments
bodyText: In lieu of paying the Security Deposit in full prior to occupancy, Tenant has elected to pay the Security Deposit in installments of [specify installment amount] due [specify schedule, e.g. on the 1st of each month], over a period of at least six months, as permitted by Colorado law. If Tenant fails to pay an installment when due, Landlord may pursue a civil action to recover the unpaid amount, but Landlord may not terminate this Lease or pursue eviction based solely on a missed installment payment.
notes: See lease-clause-citations.csv for citation, verification-date, and research-note detail (CO).

title: Security Deposit Maximum (Landlord Reference)
bodyText: Colorado law caps the security deposit you can charge at two months' rent (C.R.S. section 38-12-102.5). This is a ceiling on what you're allowed to collect - it's not something your lease needs to tell the tenant, since stating the legal maximum only gives them a number to hold you to. The actual deposit amount you're charging this specific tenant is already captured in your lease through the Security Deposit clause. Use this as a guardrail when entering the deposit amount for a Colorado lease: if you type in more than two months' rent, that number is not enforceable.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-102.5 (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Retaliation Is Prohibited
bodyText: Colorado law prohibits taking action against a tenant - raising rent, cutting services, declining to renew, or starting an eviction - because they reported an unsafe condition, exercised a right under the lease, or joined a tenant organization (C.R.S. section 38-12-509). This applies whether or not your lease mentions it, so there's no need to include it in tenant-facing text. What matters practically: if you have an independent, legitimate reason to raise rent or not renew (the lease naturally ending, a real violation, etc.), document that reason - having a clear paper trail is what protects you if a tenant later claims a decision was retaliatory.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-509 (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Rent Can't Be Raised More Than Once a Year
bodyText: No matter what your lease says, you cannot raise a tenant's rent more than once every 12 months in Colorado (C.R.S. section 38-12-702). This applies to month-to-month tenancies as much as fixed terms. Keep this in mind if you ever build a rent-escalation or annual-increase clause - the 12-month floor overrides anything the lease tries to specify.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-702 (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: For-Cause Eviction Rules (After 12 Months)
bodyText: Once a tenant has lived in a property for 12 months or more, Colorado generally requires you to have a specific legal reason - 'cause' (like nonpayment or a lease violation) or a defined 'no-fault' reason (such as selling the property or doing major renovations, with 90 days' notice) - before you can end the tenancy or decline to renew (C.R.S. section 38-12-1301 et seq.). This does NOT apply if the property is your own primary residence or directly adjacent to it, a short-term rental, a mobile home lot, or employer-provided housing. Check which of your properties fall into an exempt category - this determines which version of the month-to-month termination clause applies.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-1301 et seq. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Never Waive a Tenant's Right to Call Police
bodyText: Colorado law makes it void for any lease to contain language that waives, discourages, or penalizes a tenant for calling police or emergency services (C.R.S. section 38-12-402). This mainly matters if you're ever tempted to add a 'crime-free housing' or repeated-nuisance-call type clause - that pattern is exactly what this law targets, and any such clause would be unenforceable.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-402 (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Confidentiality Duty for a Tenant Who Is a DV/Stalking Victim
bodyText: If a tenant qualifies for early termination as a victim of domestic violence, stalking, or sexual assault, you have a legal duty not to disclose their status or new address to anyone without their consent, except where the law specifically requires it (C.R.S. section 38-12-401/402). This obligation exists regardless of whether the lease mentions it.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-401 / § 38-12-402 (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Never Ask About Immigration or Citizenship Status
bodyText: Colorado's Immigrant Tenant Protection Act prohibits asking a tenant about their immigration or citizenship status, disclosing or threatening to disclose it, or using it to harass, intimidate, or deny housing (C.R.S. section 38-12-1201 et seq.). Violations carry real penalties - up to $2,000 per violation plus attorney's fees. Any lease provision attempting to waive these protections is void, even if the tenant agrees to it in writing.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-1201 et seq. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Attorney Fee Clauses Must Work Both Ways
bodyText: A lease clause that only lets the landlord recover attorney's fees and court costs - but not the tenant, if the tenant wins - is void under Colorado law (C.R.S. section 38-12-801(3)(a)(II)). Any attorney-fee provision needs to say the prevailing party recovers fees, not just the landlord. This was actually found and fixed in the Default by Tenant clause during this review - worth double-checking any custom clause you write yourself for the same issue.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-801(3)(a)(II) (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: If a Tenant Dies During the Lease
bodyText: Colorado's 'Letty's Act' (C.R.S. section 38-12-801(3.5)) prohibits charging liquidated damages, accelerating rent beyond the end of the month (or 10 business days after the unit is vacated, whichever is later), clawing back move-in concessions, or any other early-termination penalty when a lease ends because a tenant died. You can retain enough of the security deposit to cover any damage related to the death, and you can take possession without filing an eviction once the estate's representative surrenders the unit, or automatically 30 days after death if rent is unpaid or the unit has been cleared out.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-801(3.5) ("Letty's Act") (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Notify Tenants If Your Identity or Agent Changes
bodyText: If you (or your authorized agent) change - for example, a property changes management companies, or ownership transfers - Colorado law requires the new landlord or agent to notify each tenant within 1 business day, either in writing/electronically or by posting the new information conspicuously at the property (C.R.S. section 38-12-801(2)). This is an ongoing operational duty, not something that needs to be in the lease itself.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-801(2) (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Don't Charge for a Service You Don't Actually Provide
bodyText: Colorado's Honest Pricing law prohibits charging a fee for any service you don't actually provide (C.R.S. section 6-1-737). This is a good general check for any fee-based clause you write yourself: make sure the fee corresponds to something real.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 6-1-737 (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Offer at Least One Fee-Free Way to Pay Rent
bodyText: You can't charge a rent payment processing fee unless you also offer at least one payment method with no fee attached (C.R.S. section 6-1-737). When you list your accepted payment methods in the lease, make sure at least one of them is genuinely free to the tenant.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 6-1-737 (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Advertised Rent Must Show the Full Price
bodyText: When you advertise or list a property, Colorado's Honest Pricing law requires showing a single all-in price including mandatory fees, displayed more prominently than any broken-out fee amounts - not itemized separately (C.R.S. section 6-1-737). This applies to marketing and listings, not lease text, and becomes relevant if Steinoak ever adds a listing/marketing feature.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 6-1-737 (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Utility Billing Rules Are Still Being Clarified
bodyText: If you use a shared or master utility meter and allocate costs among tenants by formula (RUBS), Colorado now has a statutory safe harbor (C.R.S. 6-1-737(4.5), added by HB26-1013). You may allocate utility costs this way if: the total you bill across all tenants does not exceed what the utility provider charged for the whole premises; you add no markup, surcharge, or administrative fee beyond what C.R.S. 38-12-801(3)(a)(VI) allows (either 2% of the billed amount or a flat $10 per month, not both); common-area and shared-facility costs are excluded from the allocation; and the allocation method is clearly disclosed in the lease or an addendum. This replaces the interim Attorney General enforcement guidance issued in late 2025.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 6-1-737(4.5) (HB26-1013); § 38-12-801(3)(a)(VI). Status moved NEEDS_REVIEW -> VERIFIED 2026-08-27 once HB26-1013 passed, codifying the safe harbor. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Radon Disclosure Risk Changes With Lease Length
bodyText: The radon disclosure itself is required on every lease regardless of term length. But if you don't make a reasonable effort to fix elevated radon within 180 days of being notified, the consequence is different depending on the lease term: a tenant can void the lease over it if the term is longer than one year, but that specific remedy doesn't apply to a lease of one year or less (effective for leases signed on or after January 1, 2026). If you're offering a tenant a renewal longer than a year, this is a real new exposure to be aware of.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-803(3)(b). Citation supplied this round (Claude Browser follow-up, 2026-09-13) via the earlier pass that located radon-disclosure-co's § 38-12-803 - not independently re-confirmed at the (3)(b) pinpoint this round. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: You Must Accept Housing Vouchers
bodyText: Colorado law requires every residential landlord to accept applicants using a housing voucher - there is no exemption for small landlords anymore (HB25-1240 removed it). Refusing an applicant solely because they use a voucher is source-of-income discrimination and can carry penalties of $5,000 to $50,000 per violation. You can still decline a voucher applicant for legitimate, consistently-applied reasons - credit, income, rental history - just never because of the voucher itself. You also can't refuse to cooperate with the approval process (inspection, paperwork) as a way of avoiding this duty.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 24-34-502 (HB25-1240 removed the small-landlord exemption, eff. 2025-05-29) (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: How the Voucher Approval Process Actually Works
bodyText: A voucher applicant doesn't move in until the unit is inspected and the Housing Assistance Payment contract is signed - you're not required to let someone occupy the unit before that happens. If a tenant does move in early anyway, standard guidance puts them on the hook for full, unsubsidized rent until the contract is finalized - you're not left holding the shortfall. The multi-year wait some landlords worry about is the tenant's wait to be issued a voucher in the first place; once a voucher holder actually applies to your specific unit, the approval process itself typically takes days to a few weeks, not years.
notes: CO: NOT_STATUTE. Operational/practical guidance, not itself citing a statute. (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Security Deposit Rights Can Never Be Waived
bodyText: A tenant cannot waive their rights regarding return of the security deposit, whether orally or in writing - any lease provision attempting this is unenforceable (C.R.S. section 38-12-103(7)). Keep this in mind for any custom security deposit language you write yourself.
notes: CO: CITED — C.R.S. § 38-12-103(7) (Restored 2026-09-25 from lease-clause-citations-CO.csv, which still holds the same data.)

title: Alternate Housing May Be Required During Major Repairs
bodyText: This is triggered by the TENANT'S REQUEST, not automatically. If a condition materially interferes with a tenant's life, health, or safety (or is a condition under C.R.S. 38-12-505(4)(l)), and the tenant requests it, you must provide - within 24 hours of that request, at no cost to the tenant - either a comparable dwelling unit or a hotel room, your choice which.
