Naming every occupant is ordinary practice in most states; in Ohio it costs you the filing and the other side's legal bill. A 'minor tenant' is a tenant under eighteen who is not emancipated. Note that this fee award is statutory, so Ohio's general ban on attorney-fee agreements does not protect you from it.
notes: OH: R.C. 1923.05(B),(C) with the 'minor tenant' definition at 1923.01(C)(15). ADDED BY SB 237 (135th GA), effective 2025-04-09 - recent, and unlikely to be reflected in older Ohio landlord guidance. Same act added the two-year limitations period for FED actions at 1923.01(B). If Steinoak ever generates eviction filings or occupant lists, this is a hard validation rule, not an education note.

title: Ohio Prescribes the Words of Your Notice
bodyText: Most states tell you how long to wait. Ohio also tells you what to say. Every notice you give to recover residential premises must contain, printed or written in a conspicuous manner, the following statement verbatim: "You are being asked to leave the premises. If you do not leave, an eviction action may be initiated against you. If you are in doubt regarding your legal rights and obligations as a tenant, it is recommended that you seek legal assistance." Serve it at least three days before you file, by certified mail return receipt requested, by personal delivery, or by leaving it at the tenant's usual place of abode or at the premises. A notice missing this exact language will not support the action.
notes: OH: R.C. 1923.04(A). VERBATIM TEXT ADDED 2026-09-19, replacing the earlier paraphrase: confirmed via two independent official Ohio state sources (codes.ohio.gov and legislature.ohio.gov), fetched separately and returning byte-identical quoted language both times: "You are being asked to leave the premises. If you do not leave, an eviction action may be initiated against you. If you are in doubt regarding your legal rights and obligations as a tenant, it is recommended that you seek legal assistance." This is a step below this project's usual primary-text-read standard (a fetch-and-summarize tool, not a direct read of the codified text) -- reasonably reliable given two independent official sources agreed exactly, but re-verify directly against the primary text before this exact wording is ever baked into a real notice-generator feature that ships to users, not just an internal reference row. Local practice glosses 'three or more days' variously as three BUSINESS days excluding the posting date, or a full 72 hours excluding weekends and holidays; the statute itself says only 'three or more days'. R.C. 1923.06(B) prescribes a second script for the summons, but that one is court-issued.

title: Electing Out of the Civil Rights Commission Can Cost You More
bodyText: If the Ohio Civil Rights Commission issues a housing discrimination complaint against you, you - not just the complainant - may elect to move the matter into common pleas court. Think before you do. In the administrative track the commission MAY award damages and fees, and the civil penalty is capped ($10,000, rising to $25,000 with one prior violation in five years and $50,000 with two or more in seven). In court, R.C. 4112.055(D) says the court SHALL award actual damages, reasonable attorneys' fees, court costs, expert witness fees and other litigation expenses, and MAY add punitive damages - with no cap and a right to a jury. Electing out trades a capped penalty for uncapped exposure. The election must be mailed certified, return receipt requested, within thirty days of the notice.
notes: OH: R.C. 4112.055(A)(2),(D) and 4112.05(B)(5),(G)(1)(b); OAC 4112-3-05(C)(2). Current 4112.055 effective 2025-09-30, amended by HB 96 (136th GA) - the biennial BUDGET bill, which is how Ohio has repeatedly moved this body of law. Filing windows: one year for a commission charge (4112.05(B)(1)) AND one year for a private civil action (4112.055(A)(1)); the two-year figure in circulation is the EMPLOYMENT window at 4112.051 and does not apply to housing.

title: Ohio Has No Alarm Statute - the Duty Comes From Code
bodyText: Do not go looking for an Ohio smoke or carbon monoxide alarm statute for rentals. There isn't one. The duty reaches you indirectly: R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) requires you to comply with all applicable building, housing, health and safety codes that materially affect health and safety, and those codes - the Ohio Fire Code and your local ordinances - are what actually specify alarms. R.C. 5321.19(B)(1) deliberately preserves local housing, building, health and safety codes from the chapter's otherwise strong preemption, so the local layer genuinely matters here. Practical effect: your alarm obligation is whatever your jurisdiction's code says, and it can change without any bill passing.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.04(A)(1); 5321.19(B)(1). Confirmed absent from ORC on a full-chapter read of 5321 plus secondary agreement for the rest of the Code. DIFFERENT ARCHITECTURE from NE (Neb. Rev. Stat. 81-5,144) and ND (N.D.C.C. 23-13-15), which both have statutory duties - do not adapt those rows. TRAP LOGGED: OAC 3701-33-13 surfaces in search and reads like an on-point rental alarm rule; it is Chapter 3701-33 AGRICULTURAL LABOR CAMPS under R.C. 3733.42, those units are excluded from ch. 5321 by 5321.01(C)(7), and its alarm provisions sit under division (B) VOLUNTARY standards. Verified by opening the rule 2026-09-18. The specific Ohio Fire Code cite (OAC 1301:7-7) is from secondary sources - verify before quoting it to a landlord.

title: Ohio Voids Attorney-Fee Clauses Both Ways
bodyText: A prevailing-party or fee-shifting clause does nothing for you in Ohio. R.C. 5321.13(C) provides that no agreement to pay the landlord's OR the tenant's attorney's fees shall be recognised in any residential rental agreement, or in any other agreement between a landlord and tenant. Making the clause mutual does not rescue it - mutuality is the fix in some states, and it is irrelevant here. Hedging it with 'to the extent permitted by applicable law' does not rescue it either; the statute says such an agreement is not recognised, so the sentence is inoperative at best and misleading to a tenant at worst. Fees are still available to either side where a STATUTE awards them - 5321.15(C), 5321.04(B), 5321.16(C) and 4112.055(D) all do - because those are statutory awards, not agreements.
notes: OH: R.C. 5321.13(C). BROADER than K.S.A. 58-2547(a)(3) and Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1415(1)(c) because of the final limb reaching any OTHER agreement between landlord and tenant, not just the lease. Drives the decision to withhold the generic default-by-tenant from OH and use default-by-tenant-ks-ne instead.

title: Two Cure Windows Before a Bounced Payment Costs Anything
bodyText: Ohio gives you no statutory returned-check fee cap - the $30-or-10% figure you will find quoted in Ohio lease templates is R.C. 1319.16, which caps what a COLLECTION AGENCY may charge, and 1319.12(A)(2) excludes a landlord collecting its own account. Your fee rides on the lease. As for going after the tenant: recovery under R.C. 2307.61 requires a THEFT OFFENCE, which means purpose to defraud plus knowledge - insufficient funds alone is not one. On top of that the tenant has two cure windows you cannot contract away: paying within ten days of notice of dishonour defeats the presumption of knowledge (2913.11(C)(2)), and paying within thirty days of your written demand bars the civil action outright (2307.61(D)). And 2307.61(B) cuts back at you - if you pursue costs and fees and the tenant wins, you pay the tenant's fees and defence costs.
notes: OH: R.C. 1319.16; 1319.12(A)(2); 2913.11(B),(C)(2); 2307.61(A),(B),(C),(D),(H)(2)(b). 2307.61(H)(2)(b) includes the bank's charges in the 'value' that gets trebled. 2307.61(C) prescribes required notice content for the written demand - re-read section-open before building a demand-letter generator. 2913.11(A)(1)(b) defines 'check' to include ACH and card transactions, so a failed electronic rent payment is inside this framework. 2913.11 measures from 'the time of issue OR THE STATED DATE, whichever is later' - Ohio accommodates postdated checks rather than penalising them, the inverse of the ND-derived checklist row.

title: Taking Rent After Your Notice Can Void It
bodyText: The line is about WHICH PERIOD the money covers. Accepting rent for obligations already incurred at the time of your three-day notice does not waive it. Accepting rent for a FUTURE period after serving the notice waives the notice as a matter of law, and you cannot proceed on it - you start over. Holding the payment is not a safe middle ground: a landlord who sits on checks without telling the tenant they are not being accepted has accepted them. If you do not want the money, say so in writing and return it. Two further cautions: a pattern of quietly accepting late or partial rent can waive the due date in your lease, and accepting the current month's rent BEFORE you serve the notice can jeopardise the action too. A 'no waiver' clause in your lease will not save you here, because the three-day notice is jurisdictional and parties cannot confer jurisdiction by contract.
notes: OH: King v. Dolton, 9th Dist. No. 02CA0041, 2003-Ohio-2423, para 12; Bristol Court v. Jones, 4th Dist. 1994; N. Face Properties v. Lin, 2013-Ohio-2281 (12th Dist.) (holding checks silently then cashing = acceptance), citing Associated Estates v. Bartell, 24 Ohio App.3d 6; OZ Property Mgt. v. Williams, 2025-Ohio-318 (12th Dist.) (pre-notice acceptance of current month); Premiere Mgt. v. Nutt, 2010-Ohio-1255 (3d Dist.). CASE LAW, not statute (Instructions item 16). 2d, 3d, 4th, 9th and 12th Districts agree - statewide consensus, not district variation. Holdings confirmed as quoted verbatim in published opinions; individual opinions not read end to end.

title: Selling the Property Does Not Get You Off the Deposit
bodyText: Ohio has no statute transferring deposit liability to a buyer, and no safe harbour for doing it properly - unlike states where handing the deposit over plus notifying the tenant relieves you. Ohio treats a security deposit as a personal obligation in the nature of a PLEDGE between you and your tenant. The liability to return it does not run with the property. It stays with you unless the buyer either assumes the obligation or receives a credit on the purchase price for the deposits. So the thing that protects you is not moving the money - it is what the purchase and sale agreement says. Get the deposits itemised in the PSA and on the rent roll, name them, and confirm assumption or a price credit in writing. Pet and other deposits count, and get missed.
notes: OH: Castlebrook, Ltd. v. Dayton Properties Ltd. Partnership, 78 Ohio App.3d 340, 348 (2d Dist. 1992), citing Tuteur v. P. & F. Enterprises, Inc., 21 Ohio App.2d 122, 133 (8th Dist. 1970); applied in Grisham v. Meadow Ridge Cincinnati Assocs. (12th Dist.), which turned on whether a PET deposit fell inside the PSA's 'Tenant Deposit' definition and appeared on the rent roll. CASE LAW, not statute (Instructions item 16). Tuteur adopted the New Jersey pledge rule because no Ohio law existed in 1970. PRODUCT NOTE: this belongs in the ownership-transfer workflow, not only the lease. Secondary sources conflict and at least one asserts the successor is automatically liable - the statutory silence does not support that.

title: Ohio Gives You No Way to Deal With Left-Behind Belongings
bodyText: If a tenant leaves possessions behind, Ohio hands you nothing. There is no notice-and-disposal procedure for an ordinary residential tenancy - the detailed machinery of notice, valuation affidavit, county auditor sign-off and sale in R.C. 1923.12 to 1923.14 applies only to manufactured home parks. Meanwhile R.C. 5321.15(B) forbids you from seizing a tenant's furnishings or possessions for rent except under a court order, and 5321.15(C) exposes you to actual damages plus reasonable attorneys' fees if you do. The practical consequence is that there is no statutory step you can follow that makes disposal safe, so get a court order, or get the property out through the writ process rather than on your own initiative.
notes: OH: confirmed absent on FULL-CHAPTER primary reads of both R.C. ch. 5321 and ch. 1923 (2026-09-18). 5321.15(B),(C). 1923.12-.14 are park-only. There is also no post-writ duty regarding a tenant's PET left at the property - a gap worth noting separately. A commercial form vendor states 'No statute' for Ohio on this; that happens to be right, but it was confirmed here from the chapters rather than adopted from the vendor.

title: Ohio Has Four Different Small-Landlord Thresholds
bodyText: There is no general 'small landlord' concept in Ohio law. Four separate provisions use four different portfolio tests, so you have to check the one attached to the duty in front of you. Fair housing under Chapter 4112 has NO small landlord exemption at all - every landlord is covered regardless of size. The rent-escrow remedy at R.C. 5321.07(C) does not reach a landlord party to agreements covering three or fewer dwelling units WHO GIVES WRITTEN NOTICE OF THAT FACT. The active-duty stay at R.C. 1923.062(C) does not apply to a landlord operating fewer than four residential premises. And the waste receptacle duty at R.C. 5321.04(A)(5) applies only where you are party to agreements covering four or more dwelling units in the same structure. Never reuse a size-keyed clause across provisions.
notes: OH: R.C. 4112.024 (exemption list contains no portfolio test; 4112.01(A)(1) 'person' sweeps in any owner, lessor, manager or agent); 5321.07(C); 1923.062(C); 5321.04(A)(5). CONTRAST WITH KANSAS, which exempts the small landlord from fair housing entirely (K.S.A. 44-1018(b)) - Ohio does not. Caveat recorded: 4112.01 and 4112.024 were read in full, the rest of ch. 4112 was not, so an exemption elsewhere in the chapter has not been ruled out.

title: Most Ohio Limits You Expect Do Not Exist
bodyText: Ohio is a thin-statute state on money terms. There is no security deposit cap, no late fee cap, no returned check fee cap that binds a landlord, no holdover damages formula, and no required mold, radon, bed bug, meth, asbestos or flood disclosure. Your only mandated lease disclosure is the owner and agent identity under R.C. 5321.18, plus the federal lead paint requirement for pre-1978 housing. That freedom is real but it is not unlimited: R.C. 5321.14 lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable clause or limit its application, and it is the only ceiling on every one of these terms. Set numbers you could defend to a judge, because nothing else will do it for you.
notes: OH: absences confirmed on a full-chapter read of ch. 5321 plus secondary agreement across the Code; 5321.16 has no cap (the $50-or-one-month figure is the INTEREST THRESHOLD, widely misreported as a cap); 5321.18; 5321.14. R.C. 5302.30 is a SALES disclosure form and does not apply to rentals - the likeliest trap on an 'Ohio disclosure' search. Pending but NOT enacted: HB 841 (introduced 2026-04-30) would create a mold/lead/radon/CO awareness program; it would not create a disclosure duty even if passed.

title: Ohio Sets No Rent-Increase Notice Period
bodyText: Chapter 5321 contains no rent-increase notice provision at all. The '30 days' you will see quoted everywhere is R.C. 5321.17(B), which is the notice required to TERMINATE a month-to-month tenancy - a different thing. For a periodic tenancy the practical route to a higher rent is to terminate on the statutory notice and offer new terms. For a fixed-term written lease, the rent is whatever the lease says for the term, and a mid-term increase needs the tenant's agreement. If you want a defined mid-term or renewal increase mechanic, it has to be in the lease, because the statute will not supply one.
notes: OH: confirmed absent on a full-chapter read of ch. 5321; 5321.17(B). SAME ERROR SHAPE as the Nebraska row - a widely-cited notice period that is actually the termination rule being reported as a rent-increase rule.

title: Two Ohio Defaults You Are Allowed to Contract Around
bodyText: Most of Ohio's landlord-tenant rules cannot be waived - R.C. 5321.13(A) makes the whole of Chapter 5321 non-waivable except in one narrow direction. But two rules that matter to you sit OUTSIDE Chapter 5321, and both are default rules you may contract around. R.C. 5301.11 says a tenant whose building is destroyed or made unfit for occupancy through no fault of their own stops owing rent - 'unless otherwise expressly provided by written agreement or covenant' - and the tenant must surrender possession to get the benefit. And Ohio's duty to re-rent after a tenant abandons comes from case law that applies 'barring contrary contract provisions'. Because neither lives in Chapter 5321, 5321.13(A) does not protect them. R.C. 5321.14 unconscionability still does.
notes: OH: R.C. 5301.11 (Title 53 ch. 5301 Conveyances - an ADJACENT-TITLE find, invisible to a ch. 5321 read; effective 1953-10-01, sole version, unamended); Frenchtown Square Partnership v. Lemstone, 99 Ohio St.3d 254, 2003-Ohio-3648. IMPORTANT: Lemstone's holding is expressly limited to a COMMERCIAL lease - the Court said so in framing the issue - and every decision upholding a mitigation waiver is commercial. Whether a RESIDENTIAL mitigation waiver survives 5321.14 is untested. DECISION 2026-09-18 (Taylor): no mitigation waiver in the default Ohio lease; surface it here as available-but-untested. Failure to mitigate is an affirmative defence, burden on the tenant. Surrender under 5301.11 means yielding all that remains - a tenant cannot stop paying and leave belongings in place.

title: Assistance Animal Accommodation
bodyText: A service animal or other assistance animal that Tenant or an Occupant needs as a reasonable accommodation for a disability is not considered a pet under this Lease, regardless of any pet policy, breed, weight, or size restriction stated elsewhere in this Lease. Landlord will not charge a pet deposit, pet rent, additional deposit, or any other pet-related fee for an assistance animal. If the disability and the disability-related need for the animal are not readily apparent, Landlord may request reliable documentation confirming the need for the accommodation, to the extent permitted by applicable law; if the disability and need are readily apparent, Landlord will not require such documentation. Tenant remains responsible for any damage to the property caused by the animal, and for keeping the animal under control and cared for. Landlord may deny or withdraw this accommodation if the specific animal poses a direct threat to the health or safety of others, or would cause substantial physical damage to the property, that cannot be reduced or eliminated by another reasonable accommodation.
notes: R.C. §4112.02(H)(19) (general reasonable-accommodation duty); OAC 4112-5-07(C) (no extra charge for an assistance animal, tenant remains liable for damage it causes), (D) (accommodation duty), (E) (burden on landlord to establish the basis for refusal), (F) (direct-threat/undue-burden exception); OAC 4112-5-02(C) (Ohio's own definition of 'animal assistant' is unusually broad -- 'any animal which aids' a person with a disability, species-neutral and not conditioned on formal training, and is state-administrative rather than tied to the federal HUD definition, so it survives a federal HUD narrowing). Grounded doubly: this is both a federal Fair Housing Act duty (42 U.S.C. §3604(f)(3)(B); 24 C.F.R. §100.204, the same regulation this project's Kansas legal-watch already monitors) and an independently-confirmed Ohio state-regulatory duty. Deliberately drafted WITHOUT a Colorado-style criminal-misrepresentation-penalty warning sentence: Ohio's own §§955.011/955.43 were each read in full and confirmed to contain no such offense reaching private residential housing (canvass items #39/#69/#73/#75) -- unlike Colorado, which has a real statutory penalty to warn about. Also deliberately does not add a documentation-verification-procedure requirement beyond 'to the extent permitted by applicable law': Ohio has no documentation standard or verification procedure in either the ORC or the OAC (canvass items #74/#127) -- this is a right without a stated verification mechanism, so the clause's existing self-limiting language is the correct level of specificity, not an omission. Closes a gap Ohio's own research (lease-clause-decision-log-OH.md items #61, #62, #74, #127, #128, #129) had already fully confirmed but never translated into a shipped clause -- same failure shape as Minnesota's and North Dakota's earlier domestic-violence-clause gaps (asserted covered in the research, no row ever built). Surfaced during a citation-extraction review of `pet-policy`/`pet-insurance-requirement`, both of which depend on this clause existing to carve out assistance animals and had no Ohio coverage for it until now. Taylor's direction 2026-09-19: build it as the carve-out, matching the existing 6-state pattern, rather than editing the shared pet clauses' own bodyText.

title: Tenant Protection Act Notice
bodyText: California law limits the amount your rent can be increased. See Section 1947.12 of the Civil Code for more information. California law also provides that after all of the tenants have continuously and lawfully occupied the property for 12 months or more or at least one of the tenants has continuously and lawfully occupied the property for 24 months or more, a landlord must provide a statement of cause in any notice to terminate a tenancy. See Section 1946.2 of the Civil Code for more information.
notes: CA: VERBATIM STATUTORY TEXT - do not paraphrase, reword or reformat. Civ. Code s1946.2(f)(3) prescribes this exact wording and requires no less than 12-POINT TYPE. Required for any tenancy commenced or renewed on or after 2020-07-01 (mobilehome 2022-07-01), in the lease, as an addendum, or as a tenant-signed written notice. s1946.2(f)(3) also subjects the notification to Civ. Code s1632, which triggers a translated copy where the lease was negotiated primarily in Spanish, Chinese, Tagalog, Vietnamese or Korean - the app cannot satisfy s1632 by rendering English alone. Consequence of non-compliance is severe and asymmetric: s1946.2(g) makes ANY failure to comply with the section render the written termination notice VOID. This row and tpa-exemption-notice-ca are mutually exclusive - a property is covered or exempt, never both. CHOICE GROUP 'ca-tpa-coverage' (2026-09-19): tpa-notice-ca (DEFAULT) and tpa-exemption-notice-ca are alternatives - a CA lease must contain EXACTLY ONE. The current rule types do not enforce this: tpa-notice-ca is unconditionally REQUIRED, so an exempt property would get BOTH notices, contradicting each other. The default is the legally safe one - an eligible property WITHOUT the exemption notice is simply covered (s1946.2(e)(8)(B), s1947.12(d)(5)(B)) - and the exemption notice replaces it only where the owner qualifies and elects. MUST be fixed in the builder before any CA lease is generated.

title: Tenant Protection Act Exemption Notice
bodyText: This property is not subject to the rent limits imposed by Section 1947.12 of the Civil Code and is not subject to the just cause requirements of Section 1946.2 of the Civil Code. This property meets the requirements of Sections 1947.12 (d)(5) and 1946.2 (e)(8) of the Civil Code and the owner is not any of the following: (1) a real estate investment trust, as defined by Section 856 of the Internal Revenue Code; (2) a corporation; or (3) a limited liability company in which at least one member is a corporation.
notes: CA: VERBATIM STATUTORY TEXT - do not paraphrase. Identical wording is prescribed twice, at Civ. Code s1946.2(e)(8)(B)(i) and s1947.12(d)(5)(B)(i). Use ONLY where the unit is alienable separate from title to any other dwelling unit (detached SFR, condo) AND the owner is not a REIT, a corporation, an LLC with any corporate member, or mobilehome-park management. For any tenancy commenced or renewed on or after 2020-07-01 the notice MUST be in the rental agreement - s1946.2(e)(8)(B)(iii); before that date it was optional. Getting this wrong in either direction is costly: omit it on a genuinely exempt SFR and the owner loses the exemption and falls under both the rent cap and just cause; include it on a non-qualifying property and the lease misstates the law to the tenant. Note s1946.2(e)(8)(B)(iv): adding this notice to a new or renewed agreement counts as a 'similar provision' for the s1946.2(b)(1)(E) refusal-to-renew just cause. CHOICE GROUP 'ca-tpa-coverage' (2026-09-19): tpa-notice-ca (DEFAULT) and tpa-exemption-notice-ca are alternatives - a CA lease must contain EXACTLY ONE. The current rule types do not enforce this: tpa-notice-ca is unconditionally REQUIRED, so an exempt property would get BOTH notices, contradicting each other. The default is the legally safe one - an eligible property WITHOUT the exemption notice is simply covered (s1946.2(e)(8)(B), s1947.12(d)(5)(B)) - and the exemption notice replaces it only where the owner qualifies and elects. MUST be fixed in the builder before any CA lease is generated.

title: Owner or Relative Occupancy Reservation
bodyText: Landlord reserves the right to terminate this Lease, in accordance with Civil Code section 1946.2, if Landlord or Landlord's spouse, domestic partner, child, grandchild, parent or grandparent unilaterally decides to occupy the property as that person's primary residence for at least 12 continuous months. Any such termination is subject to all requirements of Civil Code section 1946.2, including the notice contents, the relocation assistance or final-month rent waiver, and Landlord's obligation to re-offer the unit and reimburse moving expenses if the intended occupant does not take occupancy within 90 days or does not occupy for 12 consecutive months.
notes: CA: OPT-IN LANDLORD RIGHT - a silent lease FORFEITS it. Civ. Code s1946.2(b)(2)(A)(ii): for leases entered into on or after 2020-07-01, the owner/relative move-in just cause is available ONLY if the tenant agrees in writing at the time, or a lease provision allows the owner to terminate on a unilateral decision to occupy. Without this clause a CA landlord subject to s1946.2 cannot use owner move-in at all without the tenant's consent. This is the same inverted pattern the CO re-audit flagged at C.R.S. 38-12-503(11) (environmental-event termination, 'if permitted by the rental agreement') and is the first confirmed recurrence in another state - the CO checklist row asked future states to look for exactly this. Do NOT ship on a property using tpa-exemption-notice-ca (exempt properties need no just cause). Guardrails not yet drafted into body text: s1946.2(b)(2)(A)(iii) bars the ground where the intended occupant already occupies a unit on the property or a similar vacancy exists; (A)(iv) requires the notice to name the occupant and their relationship and to tell the tenant they may request proof; (A)(viii) defines 'owner' by recorded-interest thresholds (25 percent, or 100 percent held among named relatives). Landlord-education row recommended.

title: Security Deposit Amount
bodyText: The security deposit for this Lease is {{security_deposit}}. Under Civil Code section 1950.5(c), Landlord may not demand or receive a security deposit, however denominated, greater than one month's rent, in addition to the first month's rent paid on or before initial occupancy. No portion of the security deposit is non-refundable.
notes: CA: Verified against Civ. Code s1950.5 current text 2026-09-19. Cap is ONE month's rent, furnished or unfurnished alike - the old two/three-month unfurnished/furnished split is gone. s1950.5(c)(6) is the operative commencement rule: the subdivision does not apply to security collected or demanded BEFORE 2024-07-01, so pre-July-2024 deposits are grandfathered at the amount lawfully collected. Two exceptions the builder must handle: (a) s1950.5(c)(5) permits TWO months' rent where the landlord is a natural person, or an LLC all of whose members are natural persons, AND owns no more than two residential rental properties with no more than four dwelling units total - but s1950.5(c)(5)(B) disapplies that exception entirely where the prospective tenant is a service member, and separately forbids refusing to rent to a service member on that account; (b) s1950.5(c)(2) permits advance payment of six or more months' rent where the lease term is at least six months. s1950.5(n) bars characterising any security as 'nonrefundable'. s1950.5(c)(4) adds a service-member written-explanation duty from 2025-04-01 for above-standard security - not yet drafted as a row. EXTEND SCREEN 2026-09-19: now supersedes the base row `security-deposit-use`, which is blocked for CA. THIRD EXCEPTION FOUND 2026-09-19: Civ. Code s1940.5(g) provides that NOTWITHSTANDING s1950.5, an owner is entitled to increase the security deposit by ONE-HALF OF ONE MONTH'S RENT where the tenant has a waterbed or other liquid-filled bedding, plus a reasonable administration fee. That sits alongside the s1950.5(c)(5) small-landlord exception and the s1950.5(c)(2) advance-rent route, and the builder must not treat one month as an absolute ceiling. See waterbed-ca.

title: Security Deposit Return
bodyText: Within 21 calendar days after Tenant vacates, Landlord shall furnish Tenant an itemized statement of any amounts deducted from the security deposit and return the balance. Landlord may deduct only for unpaid rent, repair of damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, cleaning necessary to return the unit to the level of cleanliness at the inception of the tenancy, and, if this Lease so provides, replacement of personal property or appurtenances. Landlord may not charge for ordinary wear and tear or for preexisting conditions, and may not require Tenant to pay for professional carpet or other professional cleaning unless reasonably necessary. Where deductions for repairs and cleaning exceed $125, Landlord shall include copies of bills, invoices or receipts, and photographs of the unit, with the itemized statement. Tenant may request an initial inspection during the final two weeks of the tenancy and be present for it, and Landlord shall notify Tenant in writing of that right and give at least 48 hours' written notice of the inspection.
notes: CA: Written per Instructions item 24 - the base security-deposit-return row has a BLANK states field and every prior state overrode it, so the 'screen shared base rows tagged 2+ states' step could never surface it for CA. Verified against Civ. Code s1950.5 current text 2026-09-19: (h)(1) 21 calendar days; (h)(4)(A) the $125 documentation threshold; (e)(2)(A)-(C) the wear-and-tear, preexisting-condition and professional-cleaning bars; (f)(1) the initial-inspection notice and 48-hour rule. NOT yet carried into body text and needing their own rows or app logic: s1950.5(g) photograph duties (move-in photos for tenancies beginning on or after 2025-07-01; move-out photos before and after repairs from 2025-04-01) - see edu-deposit-photo-duty-ca; s1950.5(h)(1)(A)(ii) requires ELECTRONIC return where the landlord took the deposit or rent electronically, plus a written notice of that right; s1950.5(h)(1)(C) governs multi-tenant units (check payable to all adult tenants absent a written agreement); s1950.5(h)(3) the good-faith-estimate path; s1950.5(m) bad-faith retention exposes the landlord to statutory damages of up to twice the deposit plus actual damages, with the burden of proving reasonableness ON THE LANDLORD. 'SERVICE MEMBER' DEFINED, Mil. & Vet. Code s400(d), read 2026-09-19 - the definition s1950.5(c)(4) and (c)(5)(B) import: (1) a member of the state militia CALLED OR ORDERED into active state or federal service, or (2) a member of an active OR RESERVE component of the Armed Forces WHO IS ORDERED INTO ACTIVE DUTY under federal law. So a reservist who is NOT on active orders is not a 'service member' for the deposit cap. 'Armed Forces' includes the Space Force and Coast Guard (s400(a)). The landlord's small-owner two-month exception is disapplied only for a tenant meeting this definition. MILITARY TERMINATION, added 2026-09-19: Mil. & Vet. Code s409(h) makes it a MISDEMEANOR to knowingly hold a security deposit to satisfy rent accruing after a lawful s409 military termination. See military-lease-termination-ca.

title: Rent Increase Limit
bodyText: Where this property is subject to Civil Code section 1947.12, Landlord may not increase the rent over any 12-month period by more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, measured against the lowest rent charged for the unit in the 12 months before the increase takes effect, and may not impose more than two increases in any 12-month period. Any rent discount, incentive, concession or credit is excluded from that calculation and shall be listed separately in this Lease. Landlord shall give notice of any increase as required by Civil Code section 827.
notes: CA: Verified against Civ. Code s1947.12 current text 2026-09-19. Cap is the LOWER of 5 percent plus CPI or 10 percent - not 10 percent flat, a common secondary-source simplification. The applicable CPI is the metropolitan-area CPI-U under s1947.12(g)(1), with an April-to-April measurement and an August 1 switchover under (g)(3)(B), so the permitted figure is region- and date-dependent and cannot be hardcoded. Exemptions at s1947.12(d) include the rolling 15-year certificate-of-occupancy exemption, deed-restricted affordable housing, dormitories, owner-occupied duplexes where neither unit is an ADU or JADU, and separately alienable units meeting the (d)(5) owner test plus the notice at tpa-exemption-notice-ca. Remedies s1947.12(k): overcharge damages, discretionary fees, treble for wilful conduct, 3-year limitation. s1947.12(l) voids any waiver. Municipal rent control is OUT OF SCOPE for this pass and s1947.12(d)(3) expressly yields to a stricter local cap - see edu-municipal-layer-ca. GROUP NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Rent & Fees' -> 'Rent & Payment' (session drift; 12 canonical groups are used by all nine states).

title: No Fee for Serving Notices
bodyText: Landlord shall not charge Tenant any fee for serving, posting or otherwise delivering any notice relating to this tenancy, including any notice terminating a periodic tenancy and any three-day notice to pay rent, perform covenants or quit.
notes: CA: TWO INDEPENDENT STATUTORY BASES, both read section-open. Civ. Code s1946.1(i) bars a fee for serving, posting or delivering notices under that section; CCP s1161(6) separately provides that 'a landlord or its agent shall not charge a tenant a fee for serving, posting, or otherwise delivering any notice, as described in this section', covering the s1161 three-day notice family. THE EARLIER SCOPE CAUTION IS NOW RESOLVED: I had flagged that s1946.1(i) sits inside the periodic-tenancy termination section and might not reach a CCP s1161 notice. It does not need to - s1161(6) supplies a parallel ban for that family, added by SB 611 (Stats. 2024 ch. 287), OPERATIVE 2025-02-01. Body widened. NEW TOPIC SHAPE: the same prohibition enacted twice, in two different codes, by two different vehicles. Citing only one understates coverage, and a canvass that finds one and stops will mis-scope the rule. Worth screening the eight completed states for duplicated prohibitions. No prior state has surfaced a notice-service fee ban at all. THIRD BASIS FOUND 2026-09-19: Civ. Code s1946(b) - added by the same SB 611 - independently bars a fee for serving, posting or delivering any notice described in s1946, the general periodic-tenancy termination section. So the ban now rests on s1946(b), s1946.1(i) and CCP s1161(6). The same-prohibition-enacted-repeatedly pattern is stronger than recorded: THREE parallel enactments, not two.

title: Tenant Protection Act sunsets January 1, 2030
bodyText: Both halves of California's Tenant Protection Act carry an identical sunset: Civil Code sections 1946.2(n) and 1947.12(o) each provide that the section remains in effect only until January 1, 2030, and is repealed as of that date. Both became operative in their current form on April 1, 2024.
notes: CA: Read section-open 2026-09-19. LEGAL-WATCH ITEM, highest priority in CA - on 2030-01-01 the rent cap, the just-cause regime, the mandatory s1946.2(f)(3) lease notice and the s1946.2(e)(8)/s1947.12(d)(5) exemption notice all lapse together unless extended, which would invalidate four CA rows at once. A legislative bill-tracking watch keyed to s1946.2 and s1947.12 should be live well before then. Also note s1947.12(f) requires an LAO report to the Legislature on or before 2030-01-01, which is the likely vehicle for an extension debate.

title: No pre-lease notice-of-default disclosure duty (repealed 2018)
bodyText: California no longer requires a landlord to disclose a recorded notice of default to a prospective tenant before signing a lease. Civil Code section 2924.85 imposed that duty on owners of single-family and 1-4 unit properties from January 1, 2013, but the section repealed itself on January 1, 2018 by its own terms and was not extended. A separate provision, Civil Code section 2924.8, governs notice to tenants after a notice of sale is posted and has not been examined here.
notes: CA: CONFIRMED ABSENT 2026-09-19, and the evidentiary basis is a repeal annotation plus the enacting act's own title ('An act to add AND REPEAL Section 2924.85', SB 1191, Stats. 2012 ch. 566) and the sunset in s2924.85(g) - not a full-text read of the current code index, so this is one notch below the project's CITED standard. Confirm against the current Civil Code index at sync. This row exists because the dormant lease clause foreclosure-disclosure-ca asserted the repealed duty as live; per the proof-of-absence standard a confirmed absence needs its own row or no future canvass can see it. s2924.8 remains OPEN and unread. EVIDENCE UPGRADED 2026-09-19: the SB 1191 enrolled and chaptered text on leginfo (primary) shows s2924.85(g) sunset the section on 2018-01-01 'unless a later enacted statute, that is enacted BEFORE January 1, 2018, deletes or extends that date'. THAT EXTENSION WINDOW CLOSED eight years ago - any revival now would require a fresh enactment adding a new s2924.85, and none was found. The Senate floor analysis confirms the sunset. Justia's latest published version is 2016. Strong enough to treat as confirmed; the one thing not done is viewing the current Civil Code index directly, which leginfo's robots block prevents. NOTE: a December 2025 law-firm article still describes s2924.85 as current law - another live secondary-source error. s2924.8 READ 2026-09-19 - AND IT IS NOT A LANDLORD DUTY. I had described it as 'a live landlord duty' for the legal tracker. That was wrong. s2924.8(a) puts the duty on the TRUSTEE or authorized agent (posting on the property when a notice of sale is posted under s2924f) and on the MORTGAGEE, TRUSTEE, BENEFICIARY or authorized agent (mailing to 'Resident of property subject to foreclosure sale' with the s2924b notice of sale). The landlord is the borrower in that transaction, not the notifier. So the conclusion of this row gets STRONGER, not weaker: California imposes NO current statutory duty on a landlord to tell tenants or prospective tenants about a pending foreclosure. The pre-lease landlord duty (s2924.85) is repealed; the surviving foreclosure notice to residents runs through the lender side. What s2924.8 means for a landlord, as education only: s2924.8(d) confines it to residential loans where the billing address differs from the property address - i.e. precisely non-owner-occupied rental property - so a landlord's tenants WILL receive this notice if the property goes to sale. Its prescribed text, in English and every s1632 language, tells them the new owner may offer a new lease or give a 90-day notice, must honour a fixed-term lease except in limited cases, that just-cause cities may protect them further, and that their obligation to pay rent continues. Tearing it down within 72 hours is a $100 infraction. Operative 2021-03-01. The underlying tenant protections the notice summarises - the 90-day notice and fixed-term-lease rules - are in CCP s1161b and the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, NEITHER READ; the notice describes them but is not their source. | CA 2026-09-24 follow-up: CONFIRMED against the current Civil Code Div. 3, Pt. 4, Tit. 14, Ch. 2, Art. 1 section index (Justia reproduction; leginfo blocks automated access): it runs ss2920-2944.10 with no s2924.85 (sequence 2924.8 -> 2924.9 -> 2924.10); s2924.85 appears on Justia only under the 2016 code year. No successor: the surviving s2924.8 notice is a trustee/mortgagee duty to residents, not a landlord pre-lease disclosure.

title: Security deposit photograph duties (2025)
bodyText: California requires landlords to photograph the unit in connection with security deposit deductions. For tenancies beginning on or after July 1, 2025, the landlord must take photographs immediately before or at the inception of the tenancy. Beginning April 1, 2025, the landlord must photograph the unit within a reasonable time after possession is returned and before any repairs or cleaning that will be deducted, and again after that work is completed. Photographs must be provided to the tenant with the itemized statement wherever a deduction for repairs or cleaning is made.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1950.5(g)(1)-(2) and s1950.5(h)(2)(D), read section-open 2026-09-19. Two different commencement dates that are easy to conflate - the move-OUT photo duty started 2025-04-01 and applies to existing tenancies; the move-IN photo duty attaches only to tenancies that BEGIN on or after 2025-07-01. This is product work as much as lease text: the app should be prompting for and storing these photographs, and s1950.5(h)(2)(D) allows delivery by mail, email, flash drive or a link to online photographs.

title: California municipal rent and eviction ordinances (out of scope)
bodyText: Many California cities and counties impose their own rent stabilization and just-cause eviction rules that operate alongside or instead of state law. Civil Code section 1947.12(d)(3) yields to a local cap that is stricter than the state limit, and section 1946.2(i) provides that a local just-cause ordinance adopted on or before September 1, 2019, applies instead of the state scheme, as does a later ordinance that is more protective and contains a binding local finding to that effect. A property is never subject to both a local just-cause ordinance and section 1946.2.
notes: CA: Scope flag only, NOT RESOLVED, per the state-level-only decision for this pass - same 'noted, not resolved' treatment as Denver/Boulder, Minneapolis/St. Paul and Ohio's cities. California's municipal layer is materially larger than any prior state's and the state statute expressly defers to it in both directions, so the two cannot be fully separated the way they could in CO or OH: for a covered unit in a just-cause city the state clause set may be displaced wholesale. Read section-open at s1946.2(i) and s1947.12(d)(3) 2026-09-19. This is the strongest case yet for revisiting the municipal scope boundary - stronger than the MN entry that currently holds that title.

title: Bed Bug Inspection Cooperation
bodyText: Tenant shall cooperate with any inspection to facilitate the detection and treatment of bed bugs, including the inspection of Tenant's unit and any followup inspections of surrounding units until bed bugs are eliminated, and shall provide the pest control operator with requested information necessary to facilitate detection and treatment. Landlord's entry to inspect shall comply with Civil Code section 1954.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1954.604, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. Note the statute deems entry to inspect a unit selected by the pest control operator, and followup inspections of SURROUNDING units, a 'necessary service' for s1954 purposes - so a neighbour's infestation supplies lawful grounds to enter an uninfested tenant's unit. The tenant cooperation duty is statutory, so this clause restates rather than creates it. s1954 READ 2026-09-19 - see landlord-entry-ca. The s1954.604 'necessary service' characterisation maps onto s1954(a)(2) (necessary or agreed services), so the entry right is real and the 24-hour written-notice presumption in s1954(d)(1) applies to it.

title: Bed bug duties beyond the move-in disclosure
bodyText: California imposes three bed bug duties on landlords beyond the written disclosure given before a new tenancy. A landlord may not show, rent or lease a vacant unit the landlord knows has a current bed bug infestation. There is no duty to inspect for bed bugs absent notice of a suspected or actual infestation, but an infestation evident on visual inspection counts as notice. And where a pest control operator inspects units, the landlord must notify the tenants of those units of the operator's findings in writing within two business days of receiving them; for a confirmed infestation in a common area, all tenants must be notified.
notes: CA: Civ. Code ss1954.602 and 1954.605, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. The two-business-day written notice clock runs from the landlord's RECEIPT of the operator's findings, not from the inspection, and it is an affirmative duty with no tenant-request trigger - the kind of operational habitability duty the CO re-audit found the library systematically missed. s1954.602(b) is the landlord-protective limb worth knowing: no affirmative inspection duty absent notice, but visual evidence IS notice, so 'I never looked' is not a defence. No penalty appears in the chapter as supplied; enforcement route not researched.

title: California mold: a habitability duty, not a disclosure duty
bodyText: California treats mold as a habitability matter rather than a disclosure matter. Visible mold growth is listed as a substandard condition under Health and Safety Code section 17920.3(a)(13), and Civil Code section 1941.1(a) makes a dwelling untenantable if it is a residential unit described in section 17920.3. Two limits apply: the visible mold growth must be determined by a health officer or a code enforcement officer, and mold that is minor and found on surfaces that accumulate moisture as part of their properly functioning and intended use is excluded. Separately, the mold disclosure statute at Health and Safety Code section 26147 does not operate on its own terms - section 26147(e) suspends its requirements until six months after the department adopts permissible exposure limits and health guidelines and develops remediation guidelines. A landlord is never required to conduct air or surface testing for mold.
notes: CA: REWRITTEN 2026-09-19 once H&S s17920.3 was read section-open. The earlier version of this row framed CA as possibly having NO mold obligation, which would have been the wrong conclusion - the duty exists, it just sits in habitability rather than disclosure. Both limbs now verified from primary text: s17920.3(a)(13) (mold listed, officer-determination required, minor-moisture-surface carve-out) and s26147(e) (disclosure duty contingent). The one thing still NOT verified is whether the s26103/s26105/s26130 standards were ever adopted - a factual question about departmental rulemaking, not a text question. It is widely reported they were not, and this row is drafted so that it stays accurate either way. CROSS-REFERENCE for the base habitability clause screen: s1941.1(a)'s incorporation of s17920.3 pulls a 16-item inadequate-sanitation list plus structural, wiring, plumbing, mechanical, weather-protection and fire limbs into CA's tenantability standard - far broader than the seven affirmative characteristics in s1941.1(a)(1)-(7) that a reader stopping at the enumerated list would see. Note s17920.3(a)(12) subjects insect, vermin and rodent infestation to the same officer-determination requirement as mold. ADDED 2026-09-19: Civ. Code s1941.7(a) - no s1941 or s1942 duty to repair a mold dilapidation under H&S s17920.3(a)(13) arises until the lessor HAS NOTICE of it, or if the tenant is in violation of s1941.2. s1941.7(b) permits entry to repair mold subject to s1954. So CA's mold duty is notice-triggered as well as officer-determined. RESOLVED 2026-09-19: CDPH never adopted the s26103 PELs (2005 Report to the Legislature; 2017 Statement on Indoor Dampness and Mold). The contingency has never been satisfied. The row's drafting - accurate either way - no longer needs to hedge.

title: Returned-check service charge and treble damages are alternatives
bodyText: California gives the payee of a bad check two separate remedies, and a landlord cannot have both. The service charge is capped at $25 for a first check and $35 for each subsequent one. Alternatively, the landlord may pursue treble damages, but only after mailing a written demand by certified mail that states the provisions of the statute, the amount of the check, and the amount of the service charge, and then waiting 30 days for payment. Treble damages are not less than $100 and not more than $1,500. Once a tenant becomes liable for treble damages on a check, the tenant is no longer liable for the service charge or the mailing costs on that check. A tenant is liable only once per check.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1719(a)(2), together with (h)-(k) from the partial text supplied earlier. The election point is the trap: s1719(a)(2)'s closing sentence extinguishes the service charge once treble liability attaches, so a landlord demanding both is overreaching. Three MANDATORY contents in the certified-mail demand - miss one and the treble claim fails. Partial payments within the 30 days reduce the base before trebling. s1719(h) makes the remedies mandatory upon a court; (i) lets an assignee or holder enforce them; (j)(2) caps exposure at once per check; (k) preserves Commercial Code Division 3 rights and defences including holder-in-due-course status. Routed to LANDLORD_EDUCATION rather than lease text because it is an enforcement procedure, consistent with the project's notice-and-cure routing decision.

title: Methamphetamine or fentanyl remediation order: disclosure mechanics
bodyText: Where a local health officer has issued a methamphetamine or fentanyl remediation order affecting a property, the owner's disclosure duty to prospective tenants continues until the owner receives written notice from the health officer that the property requires no further action. During that period the owner must give written notice of the order to every prospective tenant who has completed a rental application, provide a copy of the order, obtain the tenant's written acknowledgment of receipt before the rental agreement is signed, and attach the notice to the rental agreement. A prospective tenant may void the rental agreement if the owner does not do all of this.
notes: CA: H&S s25400.28(b), read section-open 2026-09-19. Routed to education because three of the four obligations are procedural and occur before signature - the lease clause alone cannot discharge them. The application-stage trigger is the one most likely to be missed by a product that only generates documents at lease time. Void-the-agreement is the remedy; no damages provision appears in the subdivision.

title: Assistance Animal Accommodation
bodyText: Landlord will make reasonable accommodations for assistance animals, which include both service animals and support animals and are not pets. Tenant will not be charged any pet fee, additional rent, additional security deposit, liability insurance requirement or other additional fee in connection with an assistance animal. No breed, size or weight limitation applies to an assistance animal. Tenant remains responsible for the cost of repairing damage the animal causes to the premises, excluding ordinary wear and tear, and for keeping the animal under control, including reasonable conditions on waste disposal and on behavior that would constitute a nuisance, provided those conditions are no more restrictive than those applied to other animals on the property and do not interfere with the animal's work. An assistance animal need not be allowed if that specific animal poses a direct threat to the health or safety of others, or would cause substantial physical damage to the property of others, and the threat cannot be sufficiently mitigated by another reasonable accommodation.
notes: CA: Written 2026-09-19 against 2 CCR ss12185 and 12005(d) (Civil Rights Council fair housing regulations, Subchapter 7 Art. 18; new section filed 1979-09-16, operative 2020-01-01). RESOLVES the Instruction 24 REQUIRED-family gap - the base assistance-animal-accommodation row is tagged KS only and was invisible to the 2+ state extend screen, exactly as it was for Ohio. CLASSIFICATION for the CO re-audit's four-way ESA test: California is INDEPENDENT AND ANIMAL-SPECIFIC, but the animal-specific layer is REGULATORY rather than statutory - arguably a fifth category the checklist does not yet have. s12005(d) expressly defines assistance animals to include SUPPORT ANIMALS providing emotional, cognitive or similar support, and s12185(c) gives them a reasonable-accommodation route in dwellings. Authority is Gov. Code s12935(a), referencing ss12920, 12921, 12926, 12926.1, 12927, 12955 and 12955.3 and Auburn Woods I HOA v. FEHC (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th 1578 - state authority throughout. This is the STRONGEST answer in the project to the ESA row the HUD withdrawal threatens: CA's support-animal coverage does not rest on HUD guidance at all and survives its withdrawal intact. INSTRUCTION 16 FLAG: this is an ADMINISTRATIVE-CODE citation, not a statute. Agency rulemaking is invisible to legislative bill-tracking, so the legal-watch workflow needs a separate Civil Rights Council rulemaking watch - same treatment as KS's K.A.R., ND's Admin. Code, SD's ARSD. SCOPE TRAP, the WY/MN pattern: 2 CCR s14331 is a near-identical assistance-animal regulation but sits in the state-programs/covered-entities article, NOT housing. Do not cite s14331 for a lease. s12185 is the housing rule. Not carried into body text, see edu-assistance-animal-documentation-ca: the s12185(b) two-permissible-questions rule, the s12185(c)(2) online-certification presumption (see the sub-cite correction below), s12185(d)(4) multiple animals, s12185(d)(7) vests and ID cards, and the s12185(d)(9)(B)-(D) individualized-assessment standard. ss12176-12180 (the general reasonable-accommodation standards and defences) and s12178(f) have NOT been read. SUB-CITE RESOLVED 2026-09-19, AND I WAS WRONG TO 'CORRECT' IT: s12185(c)(2) was read section-open and it does say, in terms, that an online certification without an individualized assessment is 'presumptively considered not to be information from a reliable third party UNDER SECTION 12178(f)'. My original note faithfully reproduced the regulation's own cross-reference; my intervening 'correction' second-guessed a correct note against an inference and should not have been made. THE MIS-CITE IS THE REGULATION'S, NOT OURS. s12178(f) is the SELF-CERTIFICATION provision; the reliable-third-party list is s12178(g) and the reliability test is s12178(h), so s12185(c)(2)'s pointer does not land where its own sentence says it does. LIKELY CAUSE, recorded as a hypothesis and not verified: s12185 was filed 9-16-2019 and has NEVER been amended, while s12178 was amended 11-19-2021 operative 1-1-2022 - a re-lettering in that amendment would leave s12185 pointing at the pre-2022 subdivision. The pre-2022 text of s12178 has NOT been seen. Do not silently repair the cite when quoting the regulation; quote it as written and footnote the discrepancy. ss12176-12180 now READ section-open 2026-09-19; s12181 (modifications, restoration, escrow) remains unread. Pen. Code s365.5 READ 2026-09-19: s365.5(c) makes it a MISDEMEANOR, fine up to $2,500, to prevent or interfere with a disabled person's rights under the section - but those rights, at (b), are admittance to 'accommodations, advantages, facilities... hotels, lodging places, places of public accommodation... and other places to which the GENERAL PUBLIC IS INVITED'. A private residential tenancy is not a place to which the general public is invited, so on its text s365.5 reaches HOTELS AND LODGING but NOT ordinary rental housing. It is also CANINE-ONLY and reaches only guide, signal and service dogs - never support animals. So California has NO criminal penalty for a landlord denying an assistance animal in a residential tenancy; the remedy runs through FEHA and 2 CCR s12176 et seq. Textual conclusion; Civ. Code s54.1, the housing-access provision s365.7 cross-refers to, remains unread. Civ. Code s54.1 READ 2026-09-19 (Disabled Persons Act). s54.1(b)(6)(A): refusing to rent to, or to let a tenant keep, a GUIDE, SIGNAL OR SERVICE DOG is a denial of equal access to housing - even where the landlord bars dogs generally (s54.1(b)(5)). s54.1(b)(6)(B): the lease MAY reasonably regulate the dog's presence outside its duties, and the tenant stays liable for proven damage. Like the Penal Code sections, s54.1 is DOG-ONLY; SUPPORT animals rest on FEHA and 2 CCR s12185 alone. s54.1(b)(3)(A): modifications at the tenant's expense may be conditioned on RESTORATION, and NO ADDITIONAL SECURITY may be required - though an escrow for restoration costs may be negotiated. s54.1(d): any ADA violation is also a s54.1 violation. Remedies are in s54.3, NOT READ.

title: Assistance animals: what a landlord may ask and require
bodyText: California limits how a housing provider may verify an assistance animal. For a service animal, only two questions may be asked: whether the person is an individual with a disability, and what disability-related task the animal has been trained to perform. The person may not be asked to demonstrate the task. Service animals need not be professionally trained or certified. Animal vests, identification cards and certificates are not by themselves documentation of a disability or of the need for an accommodation. A support animal certification bought from an online service, without an individualized assessment by a medical professional, is presumptively not reliable third-party information - but before denying the request the housing provider must give the individual an opportunity to supply information that does meet the standard. A denial for direct threat must rest on an individualized assessment of objective evidence about that specific animal's actual conduct, not on speculation, fear, or what other animals have done.
notes: CA: 2 CCR s12185(b), (c)(2), (d)(7) and (d)(9)(B)-(D), plus s12005(d)(1), read section-open 2026-09-19. The online-certification presumption at (c)(2) is the landlord-favourable limb most likely to be misapplied - it is a presumption about the RELIABILITY of one document, not a licence to deny, and the regulation expressly requires giving the tenant a chance to cure the documentation first. An individualized assessment must show the disability, describe the accommodation INCLUDING THE SPECIES, and connect the two. s12185(d)(9)(D): a dog finally determined by a court to be a 'potentially dangerous dog' or 'vicious dog' under Food & Agric. Code s31601 et seq. is PRESUMPTIVELY a direct threat - the one bright line in an otherwise individualized standard.

title: Landlord Entry
bodyText: Landlord may enter the dwelling unit only in an emergency; to make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, exhibit the unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers or contractors, or make an initial inspection under Civil Code section 1950.5(f); when Tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises; or pursuant to court order. Except in an emergency or after abandonment or surrender, Landlord will give Tenant reasonable written notice stating the date, approximate time and purpose of entry, and will enter only during normal business hours unless Tenant consents at the time of entry to a different time. Twenty-four hours is presumed reasonable notice; notice mailed at least six days before entry is presumed reasonable. No notice is required to respond to an emergency, where Tenant is present and consents at the time of entry, or after Tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit. Landlord will not abuse the right of access or use it to harass Tenant.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1954, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19 (amended by Stats. 2018 ch. 445 (SB 721), eff. 2019-01-01). Core Obligations canvass row, now answerable for CA. Details that distinguish CA from the prior eight states: the notice must state DATE, APPROXIMATE TIME AND PURPOSE - not merely 'reasonable notice'; 24 hours is a PRESUMPTION rebuttable by evidence, not a fixed period; and s1954(d)(1) supplies a second presumption for MAILED notice at six days. s1954(c)'s no-abuse/no-harass rule is a standalone duty with no prior-state analogue in the library. NOT carried into body text, deliberately: s1954(d)(2) permits ORAL notice to show the unit to purchasers if the landlord gave written notice within 120 days that the property is for sale, and then requires written evidence of entry to be left inside the unit - a conditional landlord right worth its own row; s1954(d)(3) permits an oral agreement for agreed repairs or services with entry within one week. Two entry grounds in s1954(a) are cross-references not yet read: (a)(5) Chapter 2.5 (s1954.201 et seq.) and (a)(6) H&S s17973 (Art. 2.2 inspections). Both should be screened before this row is called complete. EXTEND SCREEN 2026-09-19: now supersedes the base row `landlords-access`, which is blocked for CA. ENTRY GROUNDS CLOSED 2026-09-19: s1954(a)(5) refers to Chapter 2.5 (commencing with s1954.201), which s1954.201 states is the WATER SUBMETERING chapter for multifamily residential rental buildings - so that ground is entry for submetering purposes. s1954(a)(6) refers to H&S Art. 2.2 (s17973), the EXTERIOR ELEVATED ELEMENT (balcony) inspection regime - see edu-balcony-inspection-ca. Both were flagged unread and are now identified. SEPARATE ENTRY AUTHORITY OUTSIDE s1954: H&S s13113.7(d)(2)(A) independently authorises entry to install, repair, test and maintain smoke alarms, with its own reasonable-written-notice requirement and 24-hour presumption. A CA landlord therefore has at least two statutory entry regimes with parallel but separately worded notice rules - see alarm-duties-ca. The remaining s1954.201 et seq. sections beyond the intent provision are NOT READ.

title: Lease translation duty (five languages)
bodyText: California requires a landlord who negotiates a lease primarily in Spanish, Chinese, Tagalog, Vietnamese or Korean to deliver the tenant a full translation of the lease, including every term and condition, before the lease is signed, and to provide a notice in that language at the time and place of signing. The duty applies only to a tenancy for a period longer than one month. It does not apply where the tenant negotiated through the tenant's own interpreter, meaning an adult fluent in both languages who is not employed by or supplied through the landlord. House rules and furnishing inventories ordinarily incorporated by reference do not have to be translated, but a later document making substantial changes to the parties' rights does. The English lease governs the parties' rights; the translation is admissible only to show that no contract was formed because of a substantial difference in material terms. A tenant may rescind the lease if the landlord does not comply, and any waiver of these requirements is void.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1632, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19 (amended by SB 1103, Stats. 2024 ch. 1015, eff. 2025-01-01). This is the duty s1946.2(f)(3) and Gov. Code s8589.45(b) both invoke, now read at source. Findings that change how the app must treat it: (1) SCOPE LIMIT - s1632(b)(3) reaches a tenancy 'for a period of longer than one month' only, so a pure month-to-month tenancy is OUTSIDE the duty. That is a large carve-out nobody would guess from the cross-references in s1946.2 or s8589.45. (2) The trigger is negotiating PRIMARILY in the language, orally OR in writing - not the tenant's stated preference. (3) REMEDY IS RESCISSION of the lease, s1632(k)(1); waiver void, s1632(l). (4) s1632(g)(3) excludes matters ordinarily incorporated by reference - tenancy rules and regulations and furnishing inventories - from the 'contract' to be translated. s1632(g)(1) INCLUDES any later document making substantial changes, so a material amendment re-triggers the duty. (5) s1632(h) own-interpreter exception, with the interpreter defined as a non-minor fluent in both languages and NOT employed by or made available through the landlord. (6) s1632(i) permits retaining names, addresses, brand names, numerals, dollar amounts and dates untranslated; s1632(j) makes the ENGLISH text controlling. PRODUCT IMPLICATION, escalated not solved: for a covered lease the app must generate a complete translated lease, not a translated disclosure. That is a capability the schema and builder do not have, and it is the second half of the type-size/translation schema gap recorded in the CA decision log.

title: Lease provisions void as contrary to public policy, and the before-possession rule
bodyText: California voids two categories of lease provision outright. First, any provision by which a tenant agrees to modify or waive rights or remedies under the security deposit statute or the landlord entry statute, the right to assert a future cause of action against the landlord, the right to a notice or hearing required by law, procedural rights in litigation over the tenancy, or the right to have the landlord exercise a duty of care imposed by law to prevent personal injury or personal property damage. Second, any provision modifying or waiving any other statutory right is void unless the lease was presented to the tenant before the tenant took actual possession of the premises. That second rule does not apply to a renewal that carries forward the same provision from the agreement being renewed. Both rules apply to leases executed on or after January 1, 1976.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1953 (Hiring of Real Property chapter), primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. NOTE this is CIVIL CODE s1953, not CCP s1953 - see the cross-body citation ambiguity topic. s1953(a)(5) is the operative bar for the library's exculpation rows and it is MUCH CLOSER TO OHIO s5321.13(D) than s1668 is: it voids any waiver of the tenant's right to have the landlord exercise a duty of care imposed by law to prevent PERSONAL PROPERTY DAMAGE, which is exactly what a blanket 'Landlord is not liable for loss or damage to Tenant's personal property' clause does. s1953(a)(2) is broader still - it voids waiver of the right to assert ANY future cause of action against the lessor, which reaches blanket not-liable and landlord-indemnity limbs generally. See the CA extend manifest: this supersedes my earlier read that s1668 alone might permit a merely narrowed clause. s1953(a)(1) bars contracting around s1950.5 or s1954 at all, which is why security-deposit-cap-ca, security-deposit-return-ca and landlord-entry-ca must track the statutes rather than vary them. s1953(b) IS THE SLEEPER and has no analogue anywhere in the library: a provision modifying or waiving any OTHER statutory right is void UNLESS THE LEASE WAS PRESENTED TO THE TENANT BEFORE THE TENANT TOOK ACTUAL POSSESSION. A lease signed after move-in loses every statutory-right modification it contains. Carve-out: renewals carrying forward the same provision. This is a document-TIMING rule, not a drafting rule, and the app is the only thing that can enforce it. s1953(c): applies to leases executed on or after 1976-01-01. NOT RESOLVED: s1953(a)(4) 'procedural rights in litigation' plainly reaches some jury-waiver, venue and fee-shifting limbs, but how far is case law, not text - not researched. ss1942.1 and 1942.5, cross-referenced in s1953(b), remain unread. CONFESSION OF JUDGMENT, added 2026-09-19: CCP s1132(a) - 'a judgment by confession is unenforceable and may not be entered in any superior court', for judgments obtained or entered on or after 2023-01-01 (s1132(b)). So a confession-of-judgment or cognovit clause is dead in CA by a flat statutory bar, not merely void as a s1953(a)(4) waiver of procedural rights. Screen the base library for any such clause.

title: Disability Accommodation Requests
bodyText: Tenant, a family member, or anyone Tenant authorizes to act on Tenant's behalf may request a reasonable accommodation or reasonable modification because of a disability at any time, orally or in writing, and need not use any particular words, form or procedure. Landlord will not charge any fee, deposit or other financial contribution as a condition of receiving, processing or granting such a request. Nothing in this Lease requires Tenant to give up the right to request a reasonable accommodation or modification in the future.
notes: CA: 2 CCR ss12176(f)(1)-(3), 12176(f)(5) and 12180(a)(1), (a)(3), read section-open 2026-09-19. Three rules here bind LEASE DRAFTING directly, which is why this is a clause and not only education. s12180(a)(1): unlawful to charge a fee, additional deposit or financial contribution as a condition of receiving, PROCESSING, or granting an accommodation or modification - broader than the s12185(d)(2) animal fee ban because it reaches every accommodation, not just animals. s12180(a)(3): unlawful to request or require that an individual WAIVE THE RIGHT TO REQUEST A FUTURE accommodation or modification - a prohibited lease term, and it pairs with Civ. Code s1953(a)(2), which voids waiver of the right to assert a future cause of action. s12176(f)(5): a landlord MAY ask a tenant to use a form or follow a procedure, but MAY NOT refuse the request or refuse to engage in the interactive process because the tenant did not use it. Any library clause conditioning an accommodation on a written request on the landlord's form is unenforceable as written in CA - screen the base library for that pattern. s12176(f)(3): a request may be made at any point, including during the inquiry or application process, during the tenancy, during litigation, at or after trial, and after judgment.

title: Disability accommodations: the interactive process and inquiry limits
bodyText: When a landlord cannot immediately grant a requested accommodation or modification, California requires the landlord to engage in a timely, good-faith interactive process with the tenant. A request may not be denied for lack of information without first asking for the missing information and giving the tenant a reasonable opportunity to supply it, and undue delay in responding can itself amount to a denial. What the landlord may ask depends on what is already apparent: if the disability and the need are apparent or known, no further information may be requested at all; if only the need is unclear, the landlord may ask only for a description of the accommodation and how it relates to the disability. A landlord may never ask about the tenant's diagnosis, the severity of the disability, medical records, or medical history. A tenant can often establish disability by self-certification, such as proof of receipt of disability benefits or a credible statement. All information about a disability or a request must be kept confidential. Where the need for an accommodation arises from the landlord's own failure to maintain or repair the property as required by law, the undue-burden and fundamental-alteration defenses do not apply.
notes: CA: 2 CCR ss12176(e), 12177, 12178 and 12179, read section-open 2026-09-19. Far more operationally detailed than any prior state's accommodation rules. Items with no analogue anywhere in the library: s12176(e) CONFIDENTIALITY - disability and request information may not be shared with anyone not directly involved in the interactive process or decision, save four exceptions (needed to decide, needed to implement, written authorization, required by law). A standalone landlord duty. s12177(b) - may NOT deny for lack of information without first requesting it and allowing a reasonable opportunity to respond; s12177(e) - undue delay MAY ITSELF CONSTITUTE DENIAL; s12177(c) - must look for an equally effective alternative and must grant one that works, with the tenant's preference given significant weight; s12177(g) - a later request for the same accommodation must be considered independently of an earlier denial. s12178 tiered inquiry (a)-(e), with s12178(e)(1) barring any inquiry into diagnosis, severity, medical records or medical history; s12178(f) SELF-CERTIFICATION; s12178(g) five categories of reliable third party including peer support groups and non-medical service agencies; s12178(h) case-by-case reliability test. s12179(d)(6) - where the need arises from the owner's failure to maintain or repair as required by law, the undue-burden and fundamental-alteration defenses ARE UNAVAILABLE. s12176(f)(8) - failure to accommodate is an AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE to an unlawful detainer, and a request may be made during the eviction, at trial, or after judgment. This belongs in the legal tracker's eviction workflow, not only in the lease. s12181 (modifications: restoration, escrow, who pays) NOT READ.

title: Reasonable Modifications
bodyText: Tenant may make reasonable modifications to the premises at Tenant's expense where necessary because of a disability. Landlord may ask Tenant for a reasonable description of the proposed work and reasonable assurances that it will be done competently and that any required building permits will be obtained, but will not require that the work be done by any particular contractor. Landlord will not increase any customarily required security deposit, require a liability waiver or insurance, or require Tenant to move to a different unit, as a condition of a modification. Where it is reasonable to do so, Landlord may require Tenant to restore the interior of the premises to its prior condition at the end of the tenancy, reasonable wear and tear excepted; Landlord will not require restoration of exterior modifications or modifications to common or public use areas.
notes: CA: 2 CCR s12181, read section-open 2026-09-19 (filed 11-19-2021, operative 2022-01-01; amended 2024-01-01). Four landlord-side prohibitions in this section are lease-drafting rules, which is why this is a clause: s12181(b) - MAY NOT increase a customarily required security deposit for an individual with a disability, and may not AUTOMATICALLY require an escrow account; s12181(c) - may not require a particular contractor or builder, and it is unlawful to deny a type of modification except for undue burden or fundamental alteration; s12181(f) - MAY NOT impose liability waivers or insurance requirements as conditions on a modification (a SECOND insurance-condition ban in CA after s12185(d)(2), and this one is not animal-specific); s12181(j) - may not require the tenant to move to a different unit in lieu of allowing a modification. Restoration, s12181(a): interiors only, only where reasonable, wear and tear excepted - never exteriors, common or public use areas. Where escrow IS justified it must be negotiated, capped at the cost of restoration, paid over a reasonable period, with INTEREST ACCRUING TO THE TENANT, and the full restoration cost may never be demanded up front (six factors at s12181(b)(1)-(6)). NOT in body text: s12181(h) - where the owner is a government entity or receives federal or state affordable-housing funding, the OWNER pays and the request is handled as an accommodation; s12181(i) upkeep allocation between owner and tenant; s12181(k)-(l) alternative-design rules, where the owner pays any extra cost of its own aesthetic or workmanship preference; s12181(d)-(e) common interest developments, which override conflicting Davis-Stirling governing documents; s12181(m) not-yet-constructed purchases and H&S s17959.6. s12181(g): applies to ALL housing regardless of building age and is independent of architectural accessibility compliance.

title: Repair and Deduct
bodyText: If Tenant gives Landlord or Landlord's agent written or oral notice of dilapidations rendering the premises untenantable that Landlord ought to repair, and Landlord neglects to repair them within a reasonable time, Tenant may either repair them and deduct the cost from rent when due, so long as the cost does not exceed one month's rent, or vacate the premises, in which case Tenant is discharged from further rent and other conditions as of the date of vacating. Tenant may use this remedy no more than twice in any 12-month period. This remedy is not available where the condition was caused by Tenant's own violation of Civil Code section 1929 or 1941.2. Nothing in this Lease limits any other remedy available to Tenant.
notes: CA: Civ. Code s1942, primary text supplied by Taylor 2026-09-19. Two features that cut against how repair clauses are normally drafted: (1) ORAL NOTICE SUFFICES - s1942(a) says 'written or oral notice to the landlord or his agent, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 1962'. Any lease clause conditioning the repair-and-deduct remedy on WRITTEN notice modifies a statutory right and is therefore exposed under Civ. Code s1953(b), which voids such a modification unless the lease was presented before the tenant took possession. SCREEN RESULT: the base library was searched for active rows tagged to 2+ core states that require written notice for repairs or maintenance - ZERO hits. Clean negative, recorded so a future canvass does not redo it. (2) s1942(b) makes 30 days a REBUTTABLE PRESUMPTION of reasonableness affecting the burden of producing evidence - not a waiting period. A shorter notice is permitted where circumstances require, so a lease stating a flat 30-day rule would overstate the landlord's protection. Caps: cost not more than one month's rent, and not more than TWICE in any 12-month period. s1942(d) makes the remedy cumulative. ss1929 and 1941.2 READ 2026-09-19 - see tenant-maintenance-obligations-ca. s1962(a) also READ - the agent who may receive s1942 notice is the person disclosed under owner-identity-disclosure-ca, which makes that disclosure load-bearing for this remedy: if no agent is validly disclosed, s1962(d) deems the signing party the owner's agent for receiving notices. GROUP NORMALISED 2026-09-19: 'Maintenance & Repairs' -> 'Landlord Responsibilities' (session drift; 12 canonical groups are used by all nine states).

title: Retaliation: the 180-day window and what counts
bodyText: California bars a landlord from recovering possession, causing a tenant to quit involuntarily, increasing rent, or decreasing services within 180 days of a tenant exercising rights relating to tenantability, where the tenant is not in default on rent. The triggering events include the tenant giving repair notice, giving notice of a suspected bed bug infestation, making an oral complaint about tenantability, filing a complaint with an agency, an inspection or citation resulting from such a complaint, commencing a proceeding involving tenantability, and a judgment on tenantability against the landlord; where more than one applies, the 180 days run from the latest. A tenant may invoke this protection only once in any 12-month period.
